lessons.title: Bounded stacks and duplicate-aware partitions
lessons.summary: Recursing only on the smaller side bounds stack growth.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Recursion depth

Even with good pivots, naive quicksort can recurse O(n) deep on bad luck. The fix is simple: **recurse into the smaller side and loop on the larger**. Each recursive call is on at most half the elements, so the size at least halves with every level of nesting. However bad the pivots, at most about 20 frames can be stacked up for a million elements.

```formula reference
D ≤ ⌊log_2(n)⌋ + 1
where
D: the number of simultaneous stack frames including the initial call, for a nonempty array
n: the number of elements
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times n can be halved before reaching 1
⌊ ⌋: floor, round down to an integer
≤: less than or equal to
In words: if every nested call gets at most half the elements, there can be at most about as many of them stacked up as the number of times the input size can be halved: about 20 for a million.
```

The larger side is handled by the loop, which uses no extra stack. This bounds **space**, not time: bad pivots still cost quadratic time.

```python
def quicksort(a, lo, hi):
    while lo < hi:
        # Partition before choosing the next
        # range.
        p = lomuto(a, lo, hi)
        # Only nest recursion on the smaller
        # side.
        if p - lo < hi - p:
            quicksort(a, lo, p - 1)
            # Discard the pivot and its left
            # side.
            lo = p + 1
        else:
            quicksort(a, p + 1, hi)
            # Discard the pivot and its
            # right side.
            hi = p - 1
```

## 3-way partitioning

Real data often has many duplicates: sorting a million orders by country code, or by a status with five values. Two-way partitioning keeps re-partitioning equal keys. **3-way partitioning** (Dijkstra's Dutch national flag problem) splits into `< pivot`, `= pivot` and `> pivot`, and recurses only on the outer two.

```python
def three_way(a, lo, hi):
    pivot = a[lo]
    lt, i, gt = lo, lo, hi
    while i <= gt:
        if a[i] < pivot:
            a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]
            lt += 1
            i += 1
        # Swap from the right; recheck this
        # index.
        elif a[i] > pivot:
            a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]
            # The swapped-in item is still
            # untested.
            gt -= 1
        else:
            i += 1
    return lt, gt  # a[lt..gt] == pivot
```

```
[3, 5, 3, 1, 3, 6, 2, 3]  pivot 3
->[1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 6, 5]
         lt 2     gt 5
recurse on [1, 2] and [6, 5] only
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: sorting coins around one denomination
> You tip out a jar of coins and want them in order of value. Pick one coin, say a 20p, and push every smaller coin to the left, every larger coin to the right, and every other 20p into the middle. The middle group is finished at once: there is nothing left to sort among identical coins.
>
> **How it maps:** the chosen 20p is the pivot, the left, middle and right groups are the `< pivot`, `= pivot` and `> pivot` regions bounded by `lt` and `gt`, and only the outer groups are sorted further.
>
> **Where it stops:** a jar holds only a handful of denominations, which is the best case: every equal-value group is finished in one partition. With all-distinct keys the middle group is just the pivot, and 3-way partitioning behaves like ordinary quicksort with slightly more bookkeeping.

With k distinct key values among the n elements, randomized 3-way quicksort has an expected O(n(1 + log k)) bound; exact work also depends on key frequencies; with all keys equal, it is a single O(n) pass. Sedgewick and Bentley showed this is optimal up to a constant for inputs with many duplicates.

## Key takeaways
- Recursing only on the smaller side bounds stack growth.
- Three-way partitioning finishes equal keys immediately and recurses on the outer ranges.

## Further reading
- [Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/23quicksort/)

lessons.title: Introsort and adversarial inputs
lessons.summary: A depth budget detects excessive quicksort work and switches to heapsort.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Introsort: a worst-case guarantee

David Musser's **introsort** (1997) combines three algorithms:

1. Run quicksort (median-of-three pivots).
2. Track recursion depth. If it exceeds a budget of about twice the depth that perfect halving would need (38 levels for a million elements in libstdc++), the pivots are going badly, so switch that sub-array to **heapsort**, which is O(n log n) worst case (covered later in this module).
3. Leave small sub-arrays (16 elements or fewer in libstdc++) unsorted, then finish with one insertion sort pass over the whole array.

```formula reference
d_max = 2⌊log_2(n)⌋
where
d_max: the recursion depth at which libstdc++'s introsort gives up on quicksort for that sub-array
n: the number of elements being sorted
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n
⌊ ⌋: the floor: round down to a whole number
In words: introsort allows about twice the depth that perfect halving would need before deciding the pivots are bad.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a shortcut with a turn-back rule
> You usually drive home through back streets because they are fastest. But you set yourself a rule: if you have taken more than twice the usual number of turns, something has gone wrong (roadworks, a diversion), so for the rest of the way you take the main road, which is never quick but never terrible.
>
> **How it maps:** the back streets are quicksort, the turn count is the recursion depth, the "twice the usual" rule is the depth budget, and the main road is heapsort's guaranteed O(n log n).
>
> **Where it stops:** you abandon the whole route at once. Introsort switches only the sub-array whose budget ran out; other parts of the array carry on with quicksort, and the work already done is kept.

Since heapsort costs O(n log n) on any sub-array it takes over, the total stays O(n log n). You get quicksort's speed in the common case and an O(n log n) guarantee. C++ requires `std::sort` to be O(n log n) in the worst case since C++11, and the major standard libraries typically use introsort-style hybrids (libstdc++ and MSVC; libc++ only added the worst-case fallback in LLVM 14). .NET's `Array.Sort` is introsort too. pdqsort (covered later in this module) is a modern descendant.

## Key takeaways
- A depth budget detects excessive quicksort work and switches to heapsort.
- Deterministic pivot heuristics alone cannot guarantee safety against adversarial inputs.

## Further reading
- [Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/23quicksort/)

options.explanation: Correct (n is the number of elements). That is introsort: quicksort's work before the switch is bounded, and heapsort is O(n log n) worst case.

options.explanation: No. Recursing only on the smaller side and looping over the larger bounds the stack depth logarithmically in the input size, but bad pivots still cost Θ(n²) time.

options.explanation: Correct. Crafted inputs can force quadratic comparison growth on a million elements, creating substantial CPU work; exact counts depend on the pivot rule and input. A worst-case guarantee (introsort, pdqsort, merge sort) removes the attack.

2. For a million elements, quadratic behavior can mean hundreds of billions of comparisons under a demanding partition model; the exact count and time depend on the pivot rule, input, implementation and hardware. A few requests can saturate a server.
3. Fixes:

lessons.title: Dual pivots and quicksort trade-offs
lessons.summary: Dual pivots change comparisons and swaps; an analytic model does not prove a runtime improvement.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Variants in production

- **Dual-pivot quicksort** (Yaroslavskiy, 2009) partitions into three parts using two pivots. Java has used it for `Arrays.sort` on primitive arrays since Java 7. For the analysed unsampled algorithm on uniformly random distinct keys, it makes about 5% fewer comparisons than classic quicksort but more swaps. That model alone does not establish a runtime or cache-miss improvement for a modern Java implementation. The current JDK implementation also tracks recursion depth and falls back to heapsort, and the Java documentation describes it as O(n log n) on all data sets.

```formula reference
C_dual ≈ 1.9n ln(n)
C_classic ≈ 2n ln(n)
where
C_dual: the expected comparisons of Yaroslavskiy's dual-pivot quicksort (leading term)
C_classic: the expected comparisons of classic single-pivot quicksort (leading term)
n: the number of elements, distinct and in uniformly random order
ln(n): the natural logarithm of n (base e, about 2.718)
≈: approximately equal to, keeping only the leading term
In words: dual-pivot quicksort makes about 5% fewer comparisons in this model.
```

- **Not stable.** Partitioning swaps elements over long distances, so equal keys can be reordered. That is why Java uses quicksort only for primitives (where stability is invisible) and a merge sort for objects.

## Summary

| | Quicksort |
|---|---|
| Average time | Θ(n log n) expected |
| Worst time | Θ(n²) (introsort: n log n) |
| Extra space | O(log n) stack with smaller-side recursion |
| Stable | No |

## Key takeaways
- Dual pivots change comparisons and swaps; an analytic model does not prove a runtime improvement.
- Objects with visible ties need a stable sort; quicksort partitioning normally reorders ties.

## Further reading
- [Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/23quicksort/)
- [Analysis of Yaroslavskiy’s dual-pivot quicksort](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.7409)

2. Sorting `Person` objects by age: two people aged 30 with different names are distinguishable. Users expect a re-sort by age to keep the previous order among equal ages.

4. For primitives Java picks the fastest in-place sort, dual-pivot quicksort, with no stability promise needed.

lessons.title: Heapsort construction and extraction
lessons.summary: Build a max-heap from the last parent toward the root.
lessons.body:
Throughout this lesson, n is the number of elements being sorted, and the logarithm notation in each card is base two: how many times n can be halved before reaching 1 (about 20 for a million). O, Θ and Ω are Big O, Big Theta and Big Omega: growth rates of at most, exactly and at least, ignoring constant factors.

So far we have two O(n log n) sorts, each with a catch. Merge sort is guaranteed linear times logarithmic growth but needs O(n) extra memory. Quicksort is in place but can go quadratic. **Heapsort** removes both catches: O(n log n) in the worst case, with O(1) extra space.

Then we will ask a deeper question: could some cleverer algorithm do better than linear times logarithmic growth? The answer is no, for any algorithm that sorts by comparing elements, and the proof is one of the most elegant in computer science.

## Heapsort

Heapsort is selection sort with a better data structure. Selection sort spends O(n) finding the maximum each round. A **binary max-heap** (covered in the trees module) finds and removes the maximum in O(log n).

Recall the array layout. The heap is a tree stored level by level in the array, with no pointers; the position of a node's children is computed from its own index (the code below uses `2*i + 1` and `2*i + 2`). The node at index 1, for example, has children at indices 3 and 4.

```formula reference
c_L(i) = 2i + 1
c_R(i) = 2i + 2
p(i) = ⌊(i − 1) / 2⌋
where
i: the index (position, counting from 0) of a node in the array
c_L: function giving the left-child index from the parent index i
c_R: function giving the right-child index from the parent index i
p: function giving the parent index from the child index i (for any node except the root, which is at index 0)
⌊ ⌋: the floor: round down to a whole number
In words: a node's two children sit just after twice its index, and its parent is found by reversing that step, so the tree needs no pointers.
```

Every parent is at least as large as its children (the **heap property**). So the maximum is always at index 0.

The algorithm has two phases:

1. **Build** a max-heap in place from the array.
2. **Repeatedly** swap the root (the maximum) with the last element of the heap, shrink the heap by one, and sift the new root down to restore the heap property.

The sorted part grows from the right, exactly like selection sort.

```python
def sift_down(a, i, n):
    while True:
        # Find the largest within this heap
        # family.
        big = i
        l, r = 2*i + 1, 2*i + 2
        if l < n and a[l] > a[big]:
            big = l
        if r < n and a[r] > a[big]:
            big = r
        # No larger child means the heap is
        # valid.
        if big == i:
            return
        a[i], a[big] = a[big], a[i]
        # Continue down the displaced item’s
        # path.
        i = big

def heapsort(a):
    n = len(a)
    # phase 1: bottom-up heap build
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        sift_down(a, i, n)
    # phase 2: extract max n-1 times
    # The sorted suffix grows each pass.
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        a[0], a[end] = a[end], a[0]
        # Exclude the sorted suffix from the
        # heap.
        sift_down(a, 0, end)
```

### Trace

Input `[4, 10, 3, 5, 1]`.

**Phase 1.** Start at the last node that has a child; every node after it is a leaf, which is already a valid one-element heap. The second half of the array is all leaves, so the loop starts just before the halfway point (`n // 2 - 1`, index 1 for these 5 items) and works back to index 0.


```
i 1: 10 vs children 5, 1 -> fine
i 0: 4 vs children 10, 3 -> swap 10
     [10, 4, 3, 5, 1]
     4 vs children 5, 1 -> swap 5
     [10, 5, 3, 4, 1]   max-heap
```

**Phase 2.** Swap root to the end, sift down, repeat.

```
swap 10<->1, sift: [5, 4, 3, 1 | 10]
swap 5<->1,  sift: [4, 1, 3 | 5, 10]
swap 4<->3,  sift: [3, 1 | 4, 5, 10]
swap 3<->1:        [1 | 3, 4, 5, 10]
```

## Key takeaways
- Build a max-heap from the last parent toward the root.
- Move the root to the sorted suffix and restore the remaining heap by sifting down.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)

lessons.title: Why heap construction is linear
lessons.summary: Most heap nodes have short or zero sift-down paths.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### Why the build phase is O(n), not O(n log n)

Inserting n elements one at a time would cost O(n log n) in the worst case. The bottom-up build is cheaper because most nodes are near the bottom, where sift-down is short. About half the nodes are leaves (cost 0), a quarter are one level up (cost at most 1), an eighth cost at most 2, and so on. Lots of very short moves at the bottom and a few long ones at the top add up to fewer swaps than there are elements:

```formula reference
W < n(1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …) = n
where
W: the total number of sift-down swaps the bottom-up build can make
n: the number of elements in the heap
1/2, 1/4, 1/8: at most these fractions of the n nodes can move down at least one, two and three levels
…: "and so on": the fractions keep halving
In words: at most half the nodes can move down even one level, at most a quarter two levels, at most an eighth three, and those halving counts add up to fewer swaps than there are nodes.
```

So building the heap is O(n). For a million elements that is at most about a million swaps, not 20 million. The extraction phase then does one sift-down per extracted element, each costing O(log n), so heapsort overall is **Θ(n log n) in the worst case**.

## Key takeaways
- Most heap nodes have short or zero sift-down paths.
- Bottom-up construction is linear although separate insertions have a logarithmic worst-case cost each.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)

lessons.title: Heapsort guarantees and memory locality
lessons.summary: Iterative heapsort gives constant extra space and a worst-case guarantee.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### Properties

- **In-place**, O(1) extra memory (the iterative sift-down above needs no stack).
- **Worst case O(n log n)**, with no bad inputs to defend against.
- **Not stable.** The root swap sends elements across the array, past their equals.
- **Not adaptive.** A sorted input still costs linear times logarithmic growth (in fact, a sorted ascending array is not a max-heap, so it gets rearranged fully).

### Why it loses to quicksort in practice

On paper heapsort looks strictly better than quicksort. Heapsort can be slower on large arrays, but the ratio depends on implementation, data and hardware. Memory access and comparison counts help explain why:

- Sift-down jumps from index `i` to `2i + 1`. Near the root, frequently reused nodes may remain cached. Deeper in the heap, larger index gaps and less reuse can hurt locality; a different cache line does not by itself imply a cache miss.
- Quicksort's partition scans memory sequentially, which caches and prefetchers love.
- Heapsort also does more comparisons: the ordinary sift-down shown here compares both children at almost every level on the way down. Run on a million shuffled distinct keys, the heapsort code from the extraction unit made about 37 million comparisons, roughly 1.5 times the 25 million that randomised quicksort makes on average. The leading terms below suggest a slightly smaller ratio, about 1.44; lower-order terms still matter at practical sizes.

```formula reference
C_heap ≈ 2n log_2(n)
C_quick ≈ 1.39n log_2(n)
where
C_heap: the leading term of the comparisons the ordinary sift-down heapsort shown here makes on large random distinct keys; each descent compares both children at almost every level, and lower-order terms reduce the count at practical sizes (about 1.85n log_2(n) measured at a million keys)
C_quick: the leading term of the expected comparisons of randomised quicksort with independent uniform pivots on distinct keys
n: the number of elements
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n; about 20 for a million
≈: approximately equal to (leading term only)
In words: by leading terms alone, ordinary heapsort makes about 1.44 times as many comparisons as randomised quicksort on large random inputs; at a million keys the measured ratio is about 1.5.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: fetching books along one aisle or across storeys
> Fetching books from one aisle in shelf order is quick: you walk along and pick each one up. Fetching books whose shelf numbers keep doubling (shelf 1, then 3, then 7, then 15) soon sends you to another storey for every book, even though you fetch no more books.
>
> **How it maps:** walking along one aisle is quicksort's sequential partition scan, which caches and prefetchers handle well. The doubling shelf numbers are a sift-down path from index `i` to `2i + 1`, whose jumps grow as it goes deeper.
>
> **Where it stops:** the first few shelves near the start are visited so often that they stay "at hand" (the top heap levels stay cached), and a far jump does not always cost a cache miss. The real slowdown depends on the data size and the machine, so it has to be measured.


So heapsort is used where its guarantees matter more than its speed:

- As the **fallback inside introsort** (C++ `std::sort`, .NET), triggered only when quicksort's recursion goes too deep.
- In the **Linux kernel**, whose `sort()` in `lib/sort.c` is a heapsort: no recursion, no allocation and no worst-case input to exploit. It uses a "bottom-up" sift-down variant that, according to its source comments, needs a bit more than half as many comparisons on average as checking both children at every level.
- In embedded and real-time systems where a fixed upper bound on time and memory matters most.

## Key takeaways
- Iterative heapsort gives constant extra space and a worst-case guarantee.
- Comparison counts and nonsequential access affect speed, so benchmark claims require a workload and hardware.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)

lessons.title: The comparison-sorting decision tree
lessons.summary: Each distinct-key ordering needs a distinguishable decision-tree leaf.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## The lower bound for comparison sorts

Merge sort, heapsort and good quicksorts are all linear times logarithmic growth. Is that a coincidence of the algorithms we happened to find, or a law?

It is a law, for **comparison sorts**: algorithms that learn about the input only by asking "is `a[i] < a[j]`?". That includes every sort so far.

### The decision tree

Model any comparison sort on inputs of size n as a binary tree:

- Each internal node is a comparison, such as `a[1] < a[2]?`.
- Each branch is an answer (yes or no).
- Each leaf is a final answer: the permutation that sorts the input.

Running the algorithm on a particular input traces one path from root to leaf. The number of comparisons is the length of that path.

Here is a decision tree for sorting three elements `a, b, c`:

```
              a<b?
          yes/    \no
         b<c?      a<c?
       y/   \n    y/   \n
    a,b,c  a<c?  b,a,c  b<c?
          y/  \n       y/  \n
       a,c,b c,a,b  b,c,a  c,b,a
```

Six leaves, one per ordering. The worst-case path has 3 comparisons.

### The counting argument

1. There are **n!** (n factorial: n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1) possible orderings of n distinct elements. The algorithm must be able to output each one, so the tree needs **at least n! leaves**. (If two orderings led to the same leaf, the algorithm would rearrange them identically and get one of them wrong.)
2. A binary tree of height h (its longest root-to-leaf path) has **at most 2ʰ leaves**, because the number of nodes can at most double at each level.
3. Put the two together: the tree must be tall enough to have a leaf for every ordering.

```formula essential
2^h ≥ n!
h ≥ log_2(n!)
where
h: the height of the decision tree, which is the worst-case number of comparisons
n: the number of elements being sorted
n!: n factorial, n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1: the number of possible orderings of n distinct elements
2^h: 2 multiplied by itself h times: the most leaves a binary tree of height h can have
log_2: the base-2 logarithm, which undoes "2 to the power": log_2(8) = 3
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: h yes/no comparisons can tell apart at most 2^h orderings, so any comparison sort must make at least log_2(n!) comparisons on some input.
```

For three elements there are 6 orderings. Two comparisons can tell apart at most 4 cases, so some input needs 3, exactly what the tree above uses.

How big is that bound for large n? Throw away the smaller half of the factors in n factorial and shrink each of the rest down to half the input size: what is left is still a product of about n/2 factors, each about n/2. Its logarithm grows like n log n, so **every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case**.

```formula reference
n! ≥ (n / 2)^{n/2}
log_2(n!) ≥ (n / 2) log_2(n / 2)
log_2(n!) = Ω(n log(n))
where
n!: n factorial, the product n × (n − 1) × … × 1
n: the positive integer input size; the displayed half-factor step assumes even n of at least two (odd sizes change only the rounding)
(n / 2)^{n/2}: n/2 copies of n/2 multiplied together
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
log: the logarithm (the base does not matter inside Ω)
Ω: Big Omega: grows at least this fast, up to a constant factor
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: throwing away the smaller half of the factors and shrinking the rest to half the input size still leaves something whose logarithm grows like n log n.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: twenty questions
> In the game of twenty questions, one player thinks of something and the other may only ask yes/no questions. Each answer can at best rule out half of the remaining possibilities, so twenty questions can tell apart at most about a million things. If there are more possibilities than that, some secret cannot be pinned down in twenty questions, however clever the questioner.
>
> **How it maps:** the secret is the input's ordering (one of n factorial), each question is a comparison such as "is `a[i] < a[j]`?", and the number of questions needed in the worst case is the decision tree's height. Running out of questions before the possibilities are narrowed to one is a sort that gets some input wrong.
>
> **Where it stops:** a lucky guess can win the game early, and a sort can also finish early on some inputs, which the worst-case bound allows. And the bound covers only yes/no questions: an algorithm that asks "which of 256 buckets does this key's first byte pick?" gets far more than one bit per step, which is how counting and radix sort escape it.

## Key takeaways
- Distinct permutations require separate leaves and a worst-case logarithmic-height decision tree.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)
- [Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/22mergesort/)

1. Possible orderings of 4 distinct elements: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24.
2. Each comparison has 2 outcomes, so 4 comparisons can produce at most 16 different answer sequences, and 5 comparisons at most 32.
3. With only 16 outcomes for 24 orderings, two orderings must share an outcome. The algorithm would then apply the same rearrangement to both, so at least one comes out unsorted.

So the claim is impossible; at least 5 comparisons are needed in the worst case. Merge sort meets that bound for 4 elements: two merges of pairs (1 each) plus a final merge of 2 + 2 (at most 3) = 5.

Four Boolean comparisons distinguish at most 16 outcomes, fewer than the 20 possible interleavings.
That is the bound for sorting 6 arbitrary elements, which have 720 orderings. Merging has far fewer possible outcomes, since each list is already sorted.
Correct. 4 comparisons distinguish at most 16 outcomes, fewer than 20, while 5 can distinguish up to 32. The standard merge achieves this: at most one comparison fewer than the 6 elements.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count the possible outputs: the merged list is fixed once you choose which 3 of the 6 positions hold the left list's elements, and there are 20 such choices (as the prompt says).
2. A decision tree with height h has at most 2ʰ leaves. Height 4 gives only 16 leaves, too few for 20 outcomes; height 5 gives 32, enough. So at least 5 comparisons are needed in the worst case.
3. The standard merge uses at most one comparison fewer than the total number of elements, which is 5 here, so it is optimal for this case.

The same reasoning applies to any problem solved with yes/no tests: the lower bound is the base-two logarithm of the number of possible answers. Sorting 6 arbitrary elements has 720 possible answers and needs at least 10 comparisons; merging two sorted lists has only 20.

lessons.title: Stirling estimates and average comparisons
lessons.summary: Stirling’s formula estimates factorial growth and the comparison lower bound.
lessons.body:
Here n is the number of input elements. This unit builds on the decision-tree counting argument in the previous unit.

**Stirling's approximation**, a standard estimate of n factorial, makes the bound sharper: the minimum worst-case number of comparisons is about n log₂ n minus roughly 1.44 per element. For a million elements that is about 18.5 million comparisons, compared with the rough n log₂ n figure of about 20 million.

```formula reference
log_2(n!) ≈ n log_2(n) − 1.44n
where
log_2(n!): the base-2 logarithm of n factorial: an information lower bound on worst-case comparisons to sort n distinct elements; round upward for a whole number of comparisons
n: the number of elements
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n
1.44: log_2(e), where e ≈ 2.718 is the base of natural logarithms; it comes from Stirling's formula
≈: approximately equal to (lower-order terms dropped)
In words: the information lower bound is n log_2(n) minus about 1.44 comparisons per element.
```

So **every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case**. Merge sort and heapsort are **asymptotically optimal**: no comparison sort beats them by more than a constant factor.

The same argument works for the **average** case. A binary tree with many leaves cannot have all of them shallow: if a tree has N leaves, their average depth is at least log₂ N. A comparison sort's tree has one reachable leaf for each of the n factorial orderings of distinct keys, so averaged over all orderings it still needs about log₂(n!) comparisons, which is again Ω(n log n).

That average is taken over every distinct-key permutation being equally likely, and it also bounds the expected comparisons of correct randomised sorts. It is not a bound for every input distribution: an adaptive sort can still be linear on already sorted data, because that is only one of the many orderings being averaged.

## Key takeaways
- Stirling’s formula estimates factorial growth and the comparison lower bound.
- The uniform-permutation average also requires logarithmic decision-tree depth.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)
- [Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/22mergesort/)

The comparison lower bound constrains the average over the whole uniform input distribution, not the cost of the single sorted ordering.

lessons.summary: Merge sort’s comparison count is close to the information lower bound.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### Real numbers

The last column is the base-two logarithm of the number of orderings, rounded up. For four elements, 24 possible orderings need five comparisons in the worst case, because four yes/no answers can tell apart only 16.

| n | n! | min worst-case compares |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 6 | 3 |
| 4 | 24 | 5 |
| 5 | 120 | 7 |
| 1,000,000 | huge | ≈ 18.5 million |

How close does merge sort get? For a million elements, top-down merge sort's exact worst case (from the merge-sort units in this module) is about 18.95 million comparisons, only about 2.5% above the 18.5 million minimum. (The rough figure n log₂ n, about 19.9 million, itself overstates the true minimum by about 8%.) There is little left to win on comparison counts; real-world gains come from cache behaviour, branch prediction and exploiting existing order.

> [!note] Exact optimal sorting is hard
> For five items the bound says 7 comparisons. Plain merge sort needs 8 in the worst case. The Ford–Johnson "merge insertion" algorithm achieves 7, but finding the true minimum for every n is an open problem.

### What the bound does not say

- **It only covers comparisons.** If you can look inside the keys (use an integer as an array index, or inspect digits), the decision-tree model does not apply. That is how counting sort and radix sort run in linear time (covered later in this module).
- **It is about the worst or average case.** An adaptive sort can be O(n) on already sorted input. The bound applies to the set of all n! inputs; a more refined version says you need about log₂(number of possible inputs) comparisons, which is why sorting data with few runs or few distinct values can be faster.
- **It has consequences elsewhere.** Anything that would let you sort is also Ω(n log n). For example, building a binary search tree from n items and reading it in order sorts them, so building a comparison-based BST from arbitrary distinct unsorted keys has Ω(n log n) worst-case cost.
- **The same counting bounds searching.** A sorted array of n keys has one more possible insertion position than it has keys. Each yes/no order test can at best halve the remaining positions, so finding where a new key belongs needs about log₂ n tests in the worst case: 10 tests for 1,023 keys (1,024 positions). Lower-bound binary search achieves exactly that.

```formula reference
q ≥ ⌈log_2(n + 1)⌉
where
q: the worst-case number of yes/no order tests needed to find where a new key belongs
n: the number of elements already in the sorted array, which leaves n + 1 possible insertion positions
log_2: the base-2 logarithm
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to the next whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: each yes/no test can at best halve the possible positions, so choosing among all the insertion positions needs about as many tests as the number of times their count can be halved.
```

## Key takeaways
- Merge sort’s comparison count is close to the information lower bound.
- The bound covers comparison-based worst or uniform-average cases, rather than sorted inputs or digit-indexing methods.

## Further reading
- [Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/24pq/)
- [Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/22mergesort/)

questions.prompt:
The Ω(n log n) worst-case lower bound applies to which of these algorithms? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Merge sort

options.text: Insertion sort
options.explanation: Correct. It is a comparison sort. Its worst case, Θ(n²), is above the bound, which is consistent; the bound is a floor, not a ceiling.

options.text: Counting sort
options.explanation: No. Counting sort uses keys as array indices rather than comparing them, so the decision-tree model doesn't describe it.

options.text: Heapsort
options.explanation: Correct. It is a comparison sort and matches the bound with Θ(n log n).

options.text: LSD radix sort

The bound covers algorithms whose **only** way to learn about the order is comparing pairs.

| Algorithm | Comparison sort? | Worst case |
|---|---|---|
| Merge sort | Yes | O(n log n) |
| Insertion sort | Yes | Quadratic |
| Heapsort | Yes | O(n log n) |

questions.prompt: A vendor claims their new comparison-based sort handles **any** input of 1,000,000 distinct keys with at most 15 million comparisons. What should you conclude?

options.text: It's plausible: 15 million exceeds the one million input size
options.explanation: Being above n isn't enough. The lower bound is the base-2 logarithm of n! (the number of orderings of n keys), which is far bigger than n.

options.text: It's plausible if they use a clever pivot
options.explanation: No pivot strategy beats the information-theoretic bound; it applies to every comparison sort.

options.text: It's impossible: any comparison sort needs at least about 18.5 million comparisons in the worst case
options.explanation: Correct. There are 10⁶! orderings and 15 million comparisons can distinguish at most the number of leaves in a height-15-million binary tree, which is fewer. The claim must be wrong (or the sort isn't purely comparison-based, or it only works on special inputs).

options.text: It's impossible because any sort needs quadratic comparisons
options.explanation: Quadratic cost in the input size applies to simple sorts like insertion sort, not to all sorts. Merge sort needs at most about 19 million here.

questions.workedExample:
1. Number of possible orderings of one million distinct keys: one million factorial.
2. Stirling's approximation puts the base-2 logarithm of that number at about n log₂ n minus 1.44 per key: about 19.9 million minus 1.4 million, roughly 18.5 million.
3. A decision tree of height 15 million has at most 2 to the power 15 million leaves, which is far fewer than the number of orderings. Some pair of orderings would reach the same leaf and be sorted the same way, so one of them would come out wrong.

The claim is impossible for a general comparison sort on arbitrary inputs. Perhaps they measured on nearly sorted inputs, or they're using radix-style tricks that are not pure comparisons.

questions.prompt:
A colleague says they've designed a comparison-based priority queue with O(1) `insert` and O(1) `extract_min`, both worst case. Why must this be wrong?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Priority queues can't be implemented in arrays
options.explanation: They can: a binary heap is an array. The issue is with the time bounds.

options.text: Because you could then sort n items in O(n) time with comparisons alone, violating the Ω(n log n) lower bound
options.explanation: Correct. Insert all n items (O(n)) then extract the minimum n times (O(n)) and you have a comparison sort in O(n), which is impossible.

options.text: Because extract_min must always scan every element
options.explanation: Not necessarily: a heap finds the minimum in O(1) and removes it in O(log n). It's the combination of both operations being O(1) that's impossible.

options.text: Because O(1) insert is impossible for any data structure
options.explanation: An unsorted list has O(1) insert. Fibonacci heaps even have O(1) amortised insert; their extract_min is O(log n) amortised.

questions.workedExample:
This is a **reduction** to sorting:

```
for x in items:   pq.insert(x)
out = [pq.extract_min()
       for _ in items]
```

1. With constant-time operations, n inserts plus n extractions cost only linear time in total.
2. The output is the items in sorted order, and the priority queue learnt their order using only comparisons.
3. But every comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Contradiction.

So at least one of the operations must cost Ω(log n) (amortised). Binary heaps pay O(log n) for both; Fibonacci heaps make insert O(1) amortised but extract_min stays O(log n).

questions.prompt:
Which statements about the comparison-sort lower bound are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: It also applies to the average case, not just the worst case
options.explanation: Correct. In any binary tree the average leaf depth is at least the base-2 logarithm of the number of leaves, so the average over all n! orderings of n inputs is also Ω(n log n).

options.text: Radix sort running in linear time shows the proof is flawed
options.explanation: No. Radix sort isn't a comparison sort, so the decision-tree model never applied to it. The proof is sound for its stated model.

options.text: An adaptive sort that runs in O(n) on already sorted input doesn't contradict it
options.explanation: Correct. The bound is over all n! inputs; individual easy inputs can be handled in O(n). Timsort does exactly this.

options.text: For large n, top-down merge sort's worst case is within a few per cent of the bound
options.explanation: Correct. For a million elements its exact worst case is about 18.95 million comparisons against a minimum of about 18.5 million: roughly 2.5% more.

options.text: It applies to any algorithm, including those that hash keys or use them as array indices
options.explanation: No. Those operations extract more than one bit of information per step, which is exactly how counting and radix sort escape the bound.

questions.workedExample:
The proof models an algorithm as a binary decision tree in which each node is a comparison.

- **Average case:** the leaves cover every permutation, and the average leaf depth of a binary tree is at least the base-two logarithm of its number of leaves. True.
- **Radix/counting:** they index arrays with key values, a many-way branch rather than a 2-way one, so they are outside the model. The second and fifth claims are false.
- **Adaptive sorts:** the bound is about the hardest inputs. Sorted input is one easy leaf, reached after one fewer comparison than the input size. True.
- **Merge sort:** its exact worst case is very close to the information bound for large n, which is why there is little left to gain on comparison counts. True.

lessons.title: Counting sort and stable output slots
lessons.summary: Prefix counts locate each key’s output block.
lessons.body:
The last lesson proved that any sort which only *compares* elements needs Ω(n log n) comparisons, where n is the number of elements and Ω (Big Omega) means "at least this growth rate, up to a constant factor". The way around that is to stop comparing. If keys are small integers, or can be broken into small integer digits, you can use them directly as **array indices**. An index lookup answers "which of k buckets does this go in?" in one step, which is far more information than a yes/no comparison.

That is the whole trick behind counting sort, radix sort and bucket sort. The catch is that they only work when the keys have the right shape.

## Counting sort

**Assumption:** keys are integers in a known range `0..k−1`: k is the number of possible key values, and n is the number of elements.

Count how many times each key occurs, then use running totals to work out where each key's block starts in the output.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: filing exam scripts into grade trays
> A teacher sorting a class's scripts by grade A to E first counts how many scripts got each grade. If there are 3 As and 5 Bs, the As fill the first 3 places on the shelf and the Bs the next 5, so each grade's block can be marked out before a single script is moved. Then each script goes straight into its grade's block.
>
> **How it maps:** the grades are the small integer keys, the tally is the `count` array, working out where each block starts and ends is the prefix sum, and dropping a script into its block is the placement loop. Nothing is ever compared with another script.
>
> **Where it stops:** it only works because there are five grades. Sorting by exact marks out of a million would need a million trays, most of them empty; that is why counting sort needs a small key range.

```python
def counting_sort(a, key, k):
    count = [0] * k
    for x in a:
        # Count the frequency of each
        # integer key.
        count[key(x)] += 1
    # prefix sums: end of each key's slot
    for v in range(1, k):
        # Convert frequencies into block
        # endpoints.
        count[v] += count[v - 1]
    out = [None] * len(a)
    for x in reversed(a):  # keeps it stable
        # Fill each block from its last free
        # slot.
        count[key(x)] -= 1
        # Reverse input traversal preserves
        # ties.
        out[count[key(x)]] = x
    return out
```

Trace on `[2, 5, 3, 0, 2, 3, 0, 3]` with k = 6:

```
value:   0  1  2  3  4  5
count:   2  0  2  3  0  1
prefix:  2  2  4  7  7  8
```

The prefix sum says "values ≤ 3 occupy the first 7 slots", so the last 3 goes in slot 6, the next 3 in slot 5, and so on. Output: `[0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 5]`.

- **Time:** O(n + k): one pass to count, one over the k counters, one to place.
- **Space:** O(n + k) for the output and counts.
- **Stable**, because the final pass walks the input **backwards** and fills each block from its end. Walk forwards while decrementing and equal keys come out reversed. Stability is not a nicety here: radix sort depends on it.

If you are sorting bare integers (no attached data), you can skip the output array and just write each value `count[v]` times. The prefix-sum version is needed when the key is attached to a record.

### When counting sort works and when it does not

- Exam scores 0 to 100 for 2 million students: k = 101, n = 2,000,000. Linear and very fast.
- Ages, HTTP status codes, bytes (k = 256), days of the year: all good fits.
- 1,000 arbitrary 32-bit integers: about 4.3 billion possible values, so about 4.3 billion counters, whatever n is. At 4 bytes per counter that is 16 GiB (about 17.2 billion bytes) just for the counts, and the prefix-sum pass alone visits 4.3 billion counters to sort 1,000 numbers. Python lists have different, larger overhead. Hopeless.

The rule: counting sort is great when **k is O(n)** or smaller. When k is much larger than n, use radix sort.

## Key takeaways
- Prefix counts locate each key’s output block.
- Reverse placement preserves ties; the key range controls counter memory.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)

You need to sort 2 million exam results by score, where every score is an integer from 0 to 100. What is counting sort's running time here?

options.text: O(n log n), like any sort

options.text: O(n²)

options.text: O(n + k) with 101 possible key values, so effectively linear in n

A developer "simplifies" counting sort by walking the input **forwards** in the final placement loop, still decrementing `count[key]` before placing. They then use it as the digit pass in LSD radix sort. What happens?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Nothing: counting sort is stable either way
options.explanation: Forward iteration with decrementing fills each key's block from its end, so the first equal key lands last: the order of equals is reversed.

options.text: Each pass still groups by digit correctly, but equal digits come out reversed, so the radix sort produces wrongly ordered output
options.explanation: Correct. Each pass is now 'anti-stable'. Ties on the current digit reverse the order from earlier passes, so lower digits end up scrambled.

options.text: It crashes with an index error
options.explanation: The indices are the same set of slots, just filled in a different order; there's no out-of-range access.

options.text: It becomes O(n²)

Counting sort on `[(1,'a'), (0,'b'), (1,'c')]` with a forward placement loop:

```

(1,a): count[1]=2 -> out[2]
(0,b): count[0]=0 -> out[0]
(1,c): count[1]=1 -> out[1]
```

lessons.title: Stable LSD radix passes
lessons.summary: Start with the least significant digit and preserve previous lower-digit order.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Radix sort

**Idea:** break each key into digits and sort one digit at a time with a stable counting sort.

**LSD (least significant digit) radix sort** starts with the last digit and works left. Sort `[170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]` in base 10:

```
ones:  [170, 90, 802, 2, 24, 45, 75, 66]
tens:  [802, 2, 24, 45, 66, 170, 75, 90]
100s:  [2, 24, 45, 66, 75, 90, 170, 802]
```

Look at the tens pass: 802 and 2 both have tens digit 0. The ones pass had already put 802 before 2, and because the sort is stable, they keep that order. Once a pass is done, ties on the current digit are broken by the lower digits, which were sorted earlier. **Without stability, LSD radix sort gives wrong answers.**

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: sorting a deck of cards in two deals
> To put a shuffled deck in suit-then-rank order, first deal it into 13 piles by rank (ace to king) and gather the piles into one deck in rank order. Then deal that deck into 4 piles by suit, always placing each card on the bottom of its pile so the cards keep their order, and gather the suits. Every suit now comes out already in rank order, without ever comparing two cards directly.
>
> **How it maps:** rank is the less significant digit and suit the more significant one, so dealing by rank first is the ones pass and dealing by suit second is the tens pass. Keeping each pile in dealing order is stability: it preserves the rank order inside each suit.
>
> **Where it stops:** a careless deal that reverses a pile scrambles the ranks, and nothing later fixes it; that is the computer's "unstable pass" bug. A computer also does not need physical piles: a stable counting sort computes every card's final position with prefix sums.

```python
def radix_sort(a, base=256):
    if type(base) is not int or base < 2:
        raise ValueError("base >= 2")
    if any(type(x) is not int or x < 0
           for x in a):
        raise ValueError("nonnegative ints")
    if not a:
        return a
    # Start at the least significant digit.
    exp = 1
    while max(a) // exp > 0:
        digit = lambda x: (x // exp) % base
        # Keep the order established by
        # prior digits.
        a = counting_sort(a, digit, base)
        # Move to the next more significant
        # digit.
        exp *= base
    return a
```

## Key takeaways
- Start with the least significant digit and preserve previous lower-digit order.
- Every digit pass must be stable for the final ordering to be correct.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)

options.text: It doesn't matter; any sort works for each pass
options.explanation: It matters. 21 and 25 tie on the tens digit; an unstable tens pass may output 25 before 21, undoing the ones-digit order, and no later pass looks at the ones digit again.

Tens pass: both have tens digit 2, so they tie.

- **Stable:** keeps `[21, 25]`. Correct.
- **Unstable:** may output `[25, 21]`. Wrong, and no later pass will fix it, because later passes only look at higher digits.

LSD radix sort works only because each pass preserves the work of the previous ones on ties.

lessons.title: Radix width, base and pass costs
lessons.summary: Pass count depends on key width and digit base.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### What radix sort really costs

Each pass is a counting sort over one digit, so it costs O(n + b) for a digit with b possible values. Multiply by the number of passes:

```formula essential
T = O(d(n + b))
where
T: the running time of LSD radix sort
O: Big O: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor
d: the number of digits per key, which is the number of passes
n: the number of keys
b: the base: how many values one digit can take, which is the size of each pass's counter table
In words: radix sort does one pass per digit, and each pass touches every key once plus a table of b counters.
```

The cost depends on the **key width** (through d) rather than on comparisons. A comparison sort's cost instead grows with n log n, whatever the keys look like. So radix sort tends to win when keys are short and fixed-width and n is large, and tends to lose when keys are long (many digits) or n is small; measure for your own data.

For 32-bit unsigned integers with base 256 (one byte per digit): four passes cover the full key width. A 256-entry table of four-byte counters needs 1 KiB and fits in many L1 data caches; Python counter objects have different storage overhead. For 10 million keys, that is 40 million output placements across the digit passes, plus counting reads and other overhead, versus roughly 230 million comparisons for an n log n comparison sort. Those are different operations, so the counts alone do not give a speed ratio.

> [!warning] Radix sort depends on key width
> The bound above assumes each digit operation costs a constant amount. It is "linear" only because the number of digits is treated as fixed. Python arbitrary-size integer division has its own bit cost.

How many digits are there? Divide the key width by the bits in one digit: 32-bit keys in base 256 (8 bits per digit) take 4 passes, and 64-bit keys take 8. That depends on the key width, not on n, but n distinct keys need at least enough digits to tell them apart: 10 million distinct keys cannot fit in fewer than 3 bytes.

```formula reference
d = ⌈w / log_2(b)⌉
d ≥ ⌈log_b(n)⌉
where
d: the number of digits (passes)
w: the key width in bits
b: the base, the number of values one digit can take
log_2(b): the number of bits in one digit; log_2(256) = 8
log_b(n): the logarithm of n to base b: the power you raise b to in order to get n
n: the number of keys, all distinct
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to the next whole number
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: the number of passes is the key width divided by the bits per digit, rounded up, and distinct keys need at least enough digits to tell them all apart.
```

That lower bound on d does not imply an upper bound: keys can be much wider. Fixed 32- or 64-bit keys give a fixed number of passes, with at most 2³² or 2⁶⁴ distinct values.

Choosing the base is a trade-off. Base 2¹⁶ means 2 passes for 32-bit keys, but clearing 65,536 counters costs more and the table may exceed the target CPU cache. Base 2⁸ uses a smaller table. The best base depends on counter representation, hardware and workload.

## Key takeaways
- Pass count depends on key width and digit base.
- Large counter tables and arbitrary-precision digit operations change practical cost.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)

questions.prompt: An LSD radix sort with one byte per digit (base 256) sorts 100 million unsigned 32-bit keys. The keys are widened to 64 bits, with the same values. How does the radix sort's work change, and how would a comparison sort's change?

options.text: Both stay the same, because the number of keys has not changed
options.explanation: The comparison sort's count stays about the same, but radix sort makes one pass per byte of key width, so wider keys mean more passes.

options.text: Radix sort needs twice as many passes (8 instead of 4), roughly doubling its work; a comparison sort's comparison count barely changes
options.explanation: Correct. Radix passes depend on key width: 64 bits is 8 bytes. A comparison sort makes about the same number of comparisons whatever the key width, each still a single machine comparison for 64-bit integers.

options.text: Radix sort needs 64 passes, one per bit
options.explanation: That would be base 2. With one byte per digit, each pass handles 8 bits.

options.text: Radix sort's passes grow with the logarithm of the number of keys, so nothing changes
options.explanation: Pass count depends on how many digits each key has, not on how many keys there are. Wider keys mean more digits.

questions.workedExample:
1. Passes = key width ÷ bits per digit. With 8-bit digits, 32-bit keys need 4 passes and 64-bit keys need 8.
2. Each pass reads and places all 100 million keys and uses a 256-entry count table, so doubling the passes roughly doubles the work: about 800 million placements instead of 400 million, plus counting reads and other overhead.
3. A comparison sort makes about n log₂ n comparisons (a few billion here) regardless of key width; comparing two 64-bit integers is still one machine operation.

So wider keys erode radix sort's advantage. A larger base (for example 16 bits per digit) would halve the passes, but it needs a 65,536-entry count table per pass, which may exceed the target L1 cache capacity; base 256 is the common choice. The counts are different operations, so they do not establish a runtime ratio.

questions.prompt:
Which statements about the cost of radix sort are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements; d is the number of digit passes. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: LSD radix sort with d digits in base b costs O(d·(n + b))
options.explanation: Correct. Each of the d passes is a counting sort over n elements with b counters.

options.text: Distinct keys need enough digit combinations to represent every key, so key width is not free
options.explanation: Correct. Distinct keys need enough digits to tell n values apart. Radix sort wins because real keys have a fixed width and each step is a cheap index, not because logarithmic key width disappears.

options.text: A larger base is always faster, because it means fewer passes
options.explanation: No. Base 2¹⁶ halves the passes for 32-bit keys, but its 65,536-entry table costs more to clear and may exceed the target cache capacity; fewer passes do not guarantee less time.

options.text: LSD radix sort is in-place
options.explanation: No. Each stable counting pass writes into an O(n) output buffer.

options.text: MSD radix sort on strings can stop examining characters once a bucket holds a single string
options.explanation: Correct. It only looks at as many characters as needed to distinguish each string, which is why it suits variable-length keys.

questions.workedExample:
Put numbers on it for 10⁷ 32-bit keys:

| Base | Passes | Table |
|---|---|---|
| 2⁸ | 4 | 256 counters |
| 2¹⁶ | 2 | 65,536 counters |
| 2 | 32 | 2 |

Base 2 makes 32 passes: far too many. Base 2¹⁶ makes only 2 passes but with a large, cache-unfriendly table. Choose the base by measuring the actual representation, hardware and workload.

- **Cost:** d passes, each costing about n plus b for its counter table. True.
- **Key width:** 10 million distinct keys need at least 3 bytes to tell apart, so width is not free. That is a lower bound, not an upper bound: 32-bit keys use 4 bytes, and fixed-width keys give a bounded number of passes. True.
- **Larger base always faster:** false, because of the table cost above.
- **In-place:** false; each stable counting pass needs an O(n) output buffer.
- **MSD on strings:** true; a bucket with one string needs no more characters examined.

lessons.title: Radix sorting strings and signed keys
lessons.summary: MSD sorting follows distinguishing prefixes and can stop early.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### MSD radix sort and strings

**MSD (most significant digit)** radix sort starts from the first digit, splits into buckets, and recurses into each bucket. It suits variable-length strings: you can stop as soon as a bucket has one element, and you never look at characters beyond the distinguishing prefix. Stability depends on the MSD implementation; in-place variants may be unstable. Many implementations switch to insertion sort for small buckets. Sorting strings this way is the basis of suffix array construction and some fast string-sorting libraries.

### Negative numbers and floats

- **Signed integers:** flip the sign bit before sorting (XOR with `0x80000000` for 32-bit), so negatives come first.
- **IEEE-754 floats:** positive floats already sort correctly as unsigned integers. For negatives, flip all the bits; for positives, flip just the sign bit. For non-NaN IEEE binary values this maps numerical order to unsigned-key order. Specify NaN placement and whether -0.0 and +0.0 must be treated as equivalent; simple bit transforms alone do not establish that policy.

## Key takeaways
- MSD sorting follows distinguishing prefixes and can stop early.
- Signed and floating keys require an order-preserving encoding and an explicit NaN policy.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)
- [NVIDIA radix transforms and floating-point policies](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/blob/main/cub/cub/device/device_radix_sort.cuh)

questions.prompt: A radix sort reads the raw bits of signed 32-bit two’s-complement integers as unsigned keys. Which preprocessing step makes the integer order run from the most negative value through zero to the most positive?

options.text: Flip the sign bit of every key
options.explanation: Correct: the negative half moves below the nonnegative half while ordering inside each half is retained.

options.text: Leave every bit unchanged
options.explanation: Raw unsigned order places nonnegative encodings before negative encodings, so the halves appear in the wrong order.

options.text: Flip every bit of every key
options.explanation: That reverses bitwise unsigned order within each half; the integer transform only needs the sign bit flipped.

options.text: Use an unstable digit sort
options.explanation: Stability is still required for LSD passes; changing tie handling does not repair the signed-key encoding.

questions.workedExample: In two’s complement, the sign bit is one for negative integers and zero for nonnegative integers. XOR with a mask containing only the sign bit swaps those two encoding halves without rearranging the remaining bits. The resulting unsigned keys put negatives first, then nonnegatives. This is a fixed-width integer transform; floats require a different treatment and an explicit NaN policy.

lessons.title: Bucket sort and distribution assumptions
lessons.summary: Expected bucket performance depends on independent, roughly uniform keys.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Bucket sort

**Assumption:** keys are roughly **uniformly distributed** over a known range, for example floats in `[0, 1)`.

Create n buckets (one per element), each covering an equal slice of the range. Drop each element into its bucket, sort each bucket (with insertion sort), then concatenate. The bucket for a value is found by arithmetic, not comparison: multiply the value by the number of buckets and round down (`int(x * n)` in the code). With 6 buckets, 0.78 goes into bucket 4, which covers 0.667 up to 0.833.

```python
def bucket_sort(a):  # floats in [0, 1)
    n = len(a)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    for x in a:
        # Map the value to its equal-width
        # slice.
        buckets[int(x * n)].append(x)
    out = []
    for b in buckets:
        # Sort within a slice, then
        # concatenate.
        out.extend(sorted(b))
    return out
```

```
[0.78, 0.17, 0.39, 0.26, 0.72, 0.94]
6 buckets, width about 0.167
b0: []        b1: [0.17, 0.26]
b2: [0.39]    b3: []
b4: [0.78, 0.72]   b5: [0.94]
sort each, concat:
[0.17, 0.26, 0.39, 0.72, 0.78, 0.94]
```

With independent uniform input, each bucket has expected occupancy one, and the **expected** time is O(n). But it is only as good as the distribution assumption. If all values fall in one interval whose width is the reciprocal of the bucket count aligned with a bucket, one bucket receives all n values. Insertion sort there can cost O(n²); the shown Python version uses sorted(), so its worst-case bound is O(n log n). A fixed-width interval such as [0.50, 0.51) spans many buckets when n is large.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: sorting post by the first letter of the surname
> A village post office sorts letters into 26 wall slots by the first letter of the surname, then tidies each slot by hand. When surnames are spread across the alphabet, every slot holds only a few letters and the tidying is quick. If half the village is called Smith, the S slot overflows and tidying it takes most of the morning.
>
> **How it maps:** the slots are buckets, choosing a slot from the first letter is computing the bucket from the value, tidying a slot is the inner sort, and the Smith problem is skewed data piling into one bucket.
>
> **Where it stops:** a postmaster who knows the village would make more slots for common letters. Plain bucket sort uses equal-width slices fixed in advance; choosing boundaries from a sample of the data is a separate technique (sample sort).

Bucket sort ideas show up in **histogram-based** and **sample sort** algorithms: sample the data to choose bucket boundaries that split it evenly. Distributed sorts (MapReduce's TeraSort, Spark's `sortBy`) do exactly this to divide data across machines.

## When to use which

| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| Small integer range (k not much above n) | Counting sort |
| Fixed-width ints, large n | LSD radix sort |
| Strings, variable length | MSD radix sort |
| Uniform real values | Bucket sort |
| Arbitrary comparator | Comparison sort |

In real systems:

- **NumPy:** `np.sort(kind='stable')` picks its algorithm by dtype. The NumPy 1.17 release notes, which introduced it, say radix sort is used for small integer types of **16 bits or less** and Timsort for the remaining types, including 32- and 64-bit integers. (The default `kind='quicksort'` is actually introsort.)
- **GPUs:** NVIDIA CUB offers radix sorting for supported keys; histogram, scan and scatter operations parallelize well. GPU libraries also support comparison-based sorting.
- **Databases:** some analytic engines radix-sort fixed-width encoded keys (such as normalised sort keys) instead of calling a comparator per pair.

## Pitfalls

1. **Memory.** Counting and LSD radix sorts need an O(n) output buffer plus O(k) or O(b) counters. They are not in place.
2. **Small n.** Passes and buffers can outweigh radix benefits for small inputs. There is no universal crossover size: it depends on the implementation, data type and hardware, so measure.
3. **Wide or complex keys.** A composite key (last name, then first name, then date) or a locale-aware string collation requires an appropriate order-preserving encoding; ICU collation keys, for example, are byte sequences that can themselves be radix-sorted. Total key length and encoding cost matter. A comparison sort with a key function is simpler and often fast enough.
4. **Skewed data in bucket sort.** Real data is rarely uniform. Without sampling, buckets can be badly unbalanced.

## Key takeaways
- Expected bucket performance depends on independent, roughly uniform keys.
- Skew shifts work into the inner sort; library algorithms also depend on key type and implementation.

## Further reading
- [LSD and MSD radix sorting — Princeton Algorithms](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/51radix/)
- [NumPy sorting contracts](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.sort.html)
- [NumPy 1.17 historical dtype mapping](https://numpy.org/doc/1.17/release.html)
