Which of these can realistically be sorted in **linear (or expected linear) time** with a non-comparison sort? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: 10 million `uint16` sensor readings
options.explanation: Correct. There are only 65,536 possible values, fewer than the 10 million readings, so counting sort (or one or two radix passes) is linear.

options.text: 1 million IPv4 addresses
options.explanation: Correct. They are 32-bit integers: LSD radix sort with 4 byte-sized passes.

options.text: 1 million names with locale-aware collation
options.explanation: No linear-in-record-count guarantee follows for arbitrary-length names. ICU can produce byte collation keys suitable for radix sorting, but key generation and total key length must be included.

options.text: 1 million floats drawn uniformly from [0, 1)
options.explanation: Correct. Bucket sort with n buckets runs in expected O(n) on uniform data (and radix sort on the float bit patterns also works).

options.text: 1 million objects ordered by an arbitrary user-supplied comparator
options.explanation: No. If all you have is a comparator, you're in the comparison model, and the Ω(n log n) lower bound applies (n is the number of objects).

questions.workedExample:
The question to ask is: **can I turn the key into small integer digits or a computed bucket?**

- uint16: yes, directly (65,536 possible values).
- IPv4: yes, 4 bytes.
- Uniform floats: yes. The bucket is computed by multiplying the value by the number of buckets and rounding down, not by comparing (or radix sort on the float bits).
- Collated strings: byte collation keys are possible, but their lengths and generation costs are not bounded by the number of records.
- Arbitrary comparator: by definition, only comparisons are available.

questions.prompt:
Bucket sort (100,000 equal-width buckets over [0, 1), insertion sort inside each bucket) runs on 100,000 latency values scaled to [0, 1). It is far slower than expected: 99% of the values fall in [0.000, 0.001), a range that covers only 100 of the buckets. What is happening, and what is the best fix?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: bucket sort is always linear, so the slowdown must be elsewhere
options.explanation: Bucket sort is linear only in expectation when values spread roughly uniformly. This data is heavily skewed, so the assumption fails.

options.text: About 99,000 values crowd into 100 buckets of roughly 1,000 each, and insertion sort is quadratic in each bucket's size; choose bucket boundaries from a sample or a log scale instead
options.explanation: Correct. With about 990 values per crowded bucket, insertion sort does about 245,000 shifts per bucket, roughly 25 million in total, against about 100,000 operations for uniform data. Sample-based boundaries (sample sort), a log scale for latencies, or a better inner sort fix it.

options.text: The crowded buckets overflow and lose values
options.explanation: Buckets are dynamic lists; they grow. The problem is time, not lost data or errors.

options.text: It has silently become an O(n log n) comparison sort, which is all bucket sort can achieve
options.explanation: With insertion sort inside buckets, crowded buckets cost quadratic time in their size, not n log n. And with balanced buckets, bucket sort is expected linear.

questions.workedExample:
1. Each bucket covers 1/100,000 of the range, so [0, 0.001) spans 100 buckets.
2. 99% of 100,000 is 99,000 values, so each crowded bucket holds about 990 values instead of about 1.
3. Insertion sort on 990 random values does about a quarter of 990 squared shifts, roughly 245,000, so the 100 crowded buckets cost about 25 million shifts in total. Uniform data would need around 100,000 operations.

The estimated shift count is much larger, but it does not by itself establish a 250× wall-clock slowdown. Fixes: choose bucket boundaries from a **sample** of the data (sample sort), use a log scale for latencies, or use a fallback sort inside large buckets.

questions.prompt:
Why do GPU sorting libraries such as NVIDIA's CUB typically use radix sort rather than quicksort or merge sort?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Its counting and scatter passes are data-parallel, so many GPU threads can process digits concurrently
options.explanation: Correct. Each pass is a histogram (count), a prefix sum (scan) and a scatter, all of which parallelise very well. GPU comparison sorts are also useful and can be efficient; supported key types and workload determine the choice.

options.text: Radix sort uses less memory than any comparison sort
options.explanation: LSD radix sort needs an O(n) output buffer (n is the number of keys), more than in-place quicksort. Memory isn't the reason.

options.text: GPUs cannot compare numbers
options.explanation: GPUs compare numbers perfectly well; branching on those comparisons is what is expensive when threads diverge.

options.text: Radix sort is stable, and GPUs require stability
options.explanation: LSD radix sort is stable, but that's a bonus, not the reason. GPUs have no stability requirement.

questions.workedExample:
One LSD pass breaks down into three bulk operations:

1. **Histogram:** every thread counts digit values for its chunk.
2. **Prefix sum (scan):** combine the counts into output offsets; there are well-known parallel scan algorithms.
3. **Scatter:** every element is written to its computed position.

None of these needs per-element branching on comparisons, so GPU threads stay in lockstep. With 32-bit keys and 8-bit digits, that's just 4 passes over the data.

lessons.title: Timsort runs and short-range insertion
lessons.summary: Run detection exploits existing order before merging.
lessons.body:
Textbook sorts assume random input. Real data is rarely random. Log files arrive nearly sorted by timestamp. A table is re-sorted after a few rows change. Two sorted lists are concatenated. A column has five distinct values across ten million rows.

Production sorts are **hybrid sorting algorithms** engineered to exploit that structure while keeping a worst-case guarantee. Throughout, n is the number of elements, and costs use Big O notation (O(n log n) grows like n times the base-2 logarithm of n, about 20 million for a million elements). This lesson covers the two most important designs, **Timsort** and **pdqsort**, what each mainstream language uses, and the bugs that come from comparators and stability rather than the algorithms.

## Timsort

Tim Peters wrote Timsort for Python in 2002. It became the object sort in Java 7 and Android's Java libraries, and the array sort in V8 (Chrome and Node.js) since V8 7.0 in 2018; Swift's standard-library sort uses a Timsort-style run-merging design. It is a **stable, adaptive merge sort** built around **runs**.

### 1. Find natural runs

Scan for ascending or descending runs. In the original Timsort design, descending runs must be strictly decreasing before a plain reversal, because reversing equal elements breaks stability. CPython 3.14 also handles non-increasing runs by reversing equal-key subruns first, then reversing the whole run to restore tie order. The diagram below illustrates distinct keys.

```
[1, 4, 7, 9, 8, 5, 2, 3, 6]
 run A: 1 4 7 9 (ascending)
 run B: 8 5 2   (descending -> 2 5 8)
 run C: 3 6     (ascending)
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: re-shelving a returns trolley
> A librarian re-shelving a trolley of returned books first notices stretches that are already in order (someone returned a whole series together) and keeps each stretch as a block. A stretch in exactly reverse order is simply flipped. Only then are the blocks merged into place.
>
> **How it maps:** each ordered stretch is a natural run, flipping a reversed stretch is run reversal, and merging blocks is Timsort's merge phase. The more order the trolley already has, the less work is left.
>
> **Where it stops:** a librarian can eyeball a whole stretch at once, while Timsort discovers a run one comparison at a time. And flipping a stretch that contains two copies of the same book would swap those copies, which is why reversal needs care with equal keys.

### 2. Enforce a minimum run length

Merging lots of tiny runs is wasteful. CPython 3.14 computes a **minrun** between 32 and 64 for large arrays and extends short natural runs using **binary insertion sort**. For arrays shorter than 64 it detects the first run, then extends it to the whole array if needed. Other Timsort implementations use different thresholds.

On random data, most runs are extended to minrun; a final short remainder or a longer natural run can differ, and Timsort behaves like a well-tuned bottom-up merge sort.

## Key takeaways
- Run detection exploits existing order before merging.
- Reversing a descending run must preserve ties; short runs are extended with binary insertion sort.

## Further reading
- [Sorting techniques — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html)
- [CPython 3.14.0 list-sort design notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/listsort.txt)

questions.prompt:
Python's `list.sort()` is called on a list of 1,000,000 numbers that is **already sorted**. Approximately how many comparisons does Timsort make?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: About 1 million (n − 1)
options.explanation: Correct. Timsort's run detection scans the list once, finds a single ascending run covering everything, and has nothing to merge.

options.text: About 20 million (input size times its base-two logarithm)
options.explanation: That's plain merge sort's behaviour. Timsort detects natural runs, so sorted input needs no merging at all.

options.text: About 500 billion (half the squared input size)
options.explanation: Timsort has an O(n log n) worst case for n elements; it is never quadratic.

options.text: Zero, because Python caches that the list is sorted
options.explanation: Python lists don't track sortedness; Timsort has to look at every adjacent pair to discover the run.

questions.workedExample:
1. Timsort scans from the left for a run: it compares a[1] with a[0], a[2] with a[1], and so on.
2. On sorted input every comparison says "still ascending", so the run extends to the end: one comparison per adjacent pair, 999,999 in all.
3. One run on the stack: no merges.

Reverse-sorted input (with distinct elements) is equally cheap: one strictly descending run, reversed in place in time proportional to the number of elements.

questions.prompt:
Consider the original Timsort rule: reverse only **strictly** descending runs (`a[i] > a[i+1]`), with no separate handling of equal-key subruns. Why not also reverse runs like `[5, 4, 4, 3]`?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: Strictly descending runs are faster to detect
options.explanation: Detection cost is the same either way; it's one comparison per step.

options.text: Reversing would swap the two equal 4s, breaking stability
options.explanation: Correct. Reversal flips the relative order of every pair, including equal ones, which a stable sort must not do. So the run stops at the first non-strict step.

options.text: Equal elements can't be part of any run
options.explanation: They can: ascending runs are non-decreasing (`a[i] <= a[i+1]`), so equal neighbours extend an ascending run.

options.text: Because reversing a run needs O(n) extra memory
options.explanation: Reversing a run of n elements in place uses O(1) memory, not O(n): swap from both ends towards the middle.

questions.workedExample:
Label the equal elements: `[5, 4a, 4b, 3]`.

If Timsort reversed it as a whole: `[3, 4b, 4a, 5]`. Now 4b precedes 4a, the opposite of the input. Unstable.

With the strict rule, the descending run is `[5, 4a]` (4a > 4b is false, so it stops). Reversed: `[4a, 5]`. Then `[4b, 3]` starts a new run, and the merge keeps 4a before 4b.

Ascending runs can include equal keys. Modern CPython also accepts non-increasing runs by first reversing equal-key subruns, then reversing the entire run, restoring tie order.

lessons.title: Timsort merge policies and galloping
lessons.summary: Merge only adjacent runs and use a policy that bounds pending work.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### 3. Merge runs with a balanced policy

Runs are pushed onto a stack. Timsort merges only **adjacent** runs (merging non-adjacent ones would break stability) and chooses when to merge so that merges stay balanced and the stack stays small.

Classic Timsort uses run-length rules to keep pending runs growing quickly toward the bottom of the stack: each run must be longer than the two above it combined. Run lengths then grow at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers, so even a huge array leaves only a few dozen runs waiting, and merges stay roughly balanced.

```formula reference
|A| > |B| + |C|
|B| > |C|
where
A: the third run from the top of the run stack
B: the second run from the top
C: the run on top of the stack, the most recently found
|A|: the length of run A, in elements (likewise |B| and |C|)
>: greater than
In words: each pending run must be longer than the two above it combined, and the second run longer than the top one, so lengths grow at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers and the stack stays short.
```

When an inequality fails, Timsort merges runs until both hold again. With runs of 15, 20 and 30 elements (C, B, A), the first rule fails because 30 is not greater than 20 + 15 = 35, so a merge happens. Correct collapse logic must maintain the intended invariant beyond just the top three runs. Stack capacity and policies differ by implementation; CPython uses powersort.

> [!warning] A proof found a bug
> In 2015, researchers formally verifying Java's `TimSort` with the KeY tool found that the merge-collapse rules did not always restore the invariant. On specially crafted arrays of around 67 million elements, the run stack overflowed with an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Python fixed the rule; Java enlarged the stack. Since Python 3.11, CPython uses the **powersort** merge policy (Munro and Wild), which is provably near-optimal and simpler to reason about.

### 4. Gallop when one run is winning

During a normal merge, Timsort counts how many times in a row the output came from the same run. If that reaches `MIN_GALLOP` (initially 7), it switches to **galloping**: an exponential search checking positions 1, 3, 7, 15, ... then a binary search, to find how many elements it can copy in one block. Doubling probes overshoot the target in about log₂ m steps, where m is the length of the block, and binary search pins it down in about as many again: roughly twice log₂ m comparisons instead of m one-by-one comparisons.

```
A: [1 2 3 4 5 ... 1000]
B: [500.5, 2000]
normal merge: ~500 comparisons for A's head
galloping: about 18 boundary comparisons
```

If galloping stops paying off, the threshold rises; if it keeps paying off, it falls. Run detection is what makes sorting two concatenated sorted lists O(n): Timsort finds two runs and does one linear merge. Galloping then cuts that merge's comparisons further when the lists barely interleave.

### Timsort's profile

In the table, n is the number of elements and k the number of natural runs in the input.

| Input | Cost |
|---|---|
| Already sorted / reversed | O(n): one run |
| k runs | O(n(1 + log k)) adaptive bound |
| Random | O(n log n), close to merge sort |
| Merge buffer | up to half the input elements; key caching and other metadata add storage |

Timsort minimises **comparisons**, which is exactly right for Python and JavaScript, where each comparison is a dynamic call that may run user code and costs far more than moving a pointer.

## Key takeaways
- Merge only adjacent runs and use a policy that bounds pending work.
- Galloping finds copy boundaries by exponential then binary search when one run keeps winning.

## Further reading
- [Sorting techniques — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html)
- [CPython 3.14.0 list-sort design notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/listsort.txt)
- [Formal verification of Java’s TimSort — de Gouw and colleagues](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/23709/23709A.pdf)

questions.prompt:
Which statements about Timsort are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: It merges only adjacent runs, which is needed for stability
options.explanation: Correct. Merging non-adjacent runs would move elements past others with equal keys.

lessons.title: pdqsort and language sorting contracts
lessons.summary: Pattern checks and bounded insertion attempts exploit favourable inputs.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## pdqsort

Orson Peters' **pattern-defeating quicksort** (2016, paper 2021) is the modern unstable sort. Go adopted it for `sort.Sort` in Go 1.19, and Rust used it for `sort_unstable` for years (Rust 1.81 replaced it with **ipnsort**, a newer design by Peters and Bergdoll). It extends introsort with ideas that make common patterns fast:

- **Pivot selection**: median-of-three, or Tukey's ninther for larger arrays.
- **Partial insertion sort**: if partitioning detects an already partitioned range (excluding pivot setup), try insertion sort with a small cap on moves. On sorted or nearly sorted input this finishes in O(n).
- **Equal-element handling**: if the pivot equals the element just before the current sub-array, all elements equal to it are partitioned off in one pass. With k distinct keys the cost is O(nk), linear for few distinct values.
- **Bad-partition detection**: an unbalanced split triggers a shuffle of a few elements to break adversarial patterns. After a logarithmic budget of bad partitions, it falls back to heapsort, guaranteeing O(n log n).
- **Branchless block partitioning** (from BlockQuicksort) for cheap comparisons such as integers, avoiding branch mispredictions on random data. Ports differ: Go's implementation notes that it leaves out the BlockQuicksort optimisations.

The result: O(n log n) worst case, in place, and linear on sorted, reversed and all-equal inputs.

## What your language actually uses

| Language | Default | Stable? |
|---|---|---|
| Python `sorted`, `list.sort` | Timsort (powersort merge policy since 3.11) | Yes |
| Java objects, `List.sort` | TimSort | Yes |
| Java primitives | Dual-pivot quicksort | n/a |
| JavaScript `Array.sort` | Timsort in V8 | Yes |
| C++ `std::sort` | Typically introsort-family; implementation-specific | No |
| C++ `std::stable_sort` | Typically merge-based; implementation-specific | Yes |
| Rust `sort` / `sort_unstable` | driftsort / ipnsort (since 1.81) | Yes / No |
| Go `sort.Sort`, `slices.Sort` | pdqsort (`sort` since Go 1.19; `slices` since it was added in Go 1.21) | No |

Notes on the table:

- Java sorts primitives with an unstable quicksort because equal `int`s are indistinguishable, so stability is invisible. Objects need stability, so they get TimSort.
- JavaScript only **required** a stable sort from ES2019; older engines differed.
- Go provides `sort.Stable` and `slices.SortStableFunc` when you need stability.
- C's `qsort` specifies neither the algorithm nor stability.

## Key takeaways
- Pattern checks and bounded insertion attempts exploit favourable inputs.
- Know whether stability and complexity are API guarantees or implementation choices.

## Further reading
- [pdqsort design and guarantees — project documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/orlp/pdqsort/master/readme.md)
- [Go 1.19 sorting implementation change](https://go.dev/doc/go1.19)
- [Slice sorting contracts — Rust documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

lessons.title: Comparator contracts and failure cases
lessons.summary: Strict weak ordering includes transitivity of both ordering and incomparability.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Comparators: the contract

A comparator must define a **strict weak ordering**. In plain terms, its "comes before" answers must obey these rules:

1. **Consistent:** `cmp(a, b)` always gives the same answer for the same pair.
2. **Irreflexive and asymmetric:** nothing comes before itself, and two elements cannot each come before the other.
3. **Transitive:** if a comes before b and b before c, then a comes before c.
4. **Transitive ties:** if a ties with b (neither comes before the other) and b ties with c, then a must tie with c.

```formula reference
¬(a < a)
a < b  ⇒  ¬(b < a)
(a < b) ∧ (b < c)  ⇒  a < c
E(a, b) = ¬(a < b) ∧ ¬(b < a)
E(a, b) ∧ E(b, c)  ⇒  E(a, c)
where
a: any element being sorted
b: any other element
c: any third element
E: Boolean equivalence test: true when neither argument precedes the other according to this comparator; it need not mean the objects are identical
<: "comes before", as the comparator reports it
¬: "not": the statement in brackets is false
∧: "and": both statements hold
⇒: "implies": if the left side holds, the right side must too
In words: nothing comes before itself, two elements cannot each come before the other, and both ordering and comparator-equivalence chain transitively. If a ties b and b ties c, a must also tie c.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: ranking rock, paper and scissors
> Try to line up rock, paper and scissors from weakest to strongest. Rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, but paper beats rock, so whichever order you pick, some pair is in the "wrong" place. Asking different people to do the ranking gives different answers, depending on which pair each looks at first.
>
> **How it maps:** "beats" is a comparator that breaks transitivity. A sorting algorithm assumes the answers fit together into one consistent line; when they do not, its result depends on which pairs it happened to compare, or it detects the contradiction and fails.
>
> **Where it stops:** the game's cycle is obvious. Real comparator bugs are usually hidden: `a - b` is correct for most values and wrong only for extreme ones, and NaN breaks the rules only when one is present, so the failure appears rarely and often only in production.

Break the contract and the consequences depend on the language:

- **Java** TimSort may throw `IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract!`, often only on large or unlucky inputs, so it passes tests and fails in production.
- **C++** `std::sort` has **undefined behaviour**. Real implementations can run past the end of the array (the unguarded insertion loop assumes some earlier element will stop its scan), causing crashes or memory corruption.
- **Rust** may panic since 1.81, but never causes memory unsafety.
- **Python** may produce an order that does not satisfy the intended relation; user comparison code can also raise exceptions.

Common ways to break it (the Java block shows alternative comparator expressions to place inside a sorting call):

```java
// overflow: 2e9 - (-2e9) wraps negative
(a, b) -> a - b
// fix
(a, b) -> Integer.compare(a, b)
```

Why it overflows: Java's `int` holds values only up to 2,147,483,647 (about 2.1 billion). Comparing 2 billion with −2 billion gives a true difference of 4 billion, which does not fit, so it wraps round to −294,967,296. The negative result tells the sort that 2 billion comes *before* −2 billion.

- Random comparators (`() => Math.random() - 0.5` to "shuffle") are inconsistent and produce biased shuffles. Use Fisher–Yates.
- **NaN.** Ordered comparisons (<, <=, >, >=) with NaN are false, while != is true. Treating NaN as equivalent to every value via neither-less-than breaks transitivity of incomparability. In Python, `sorted([3, nan, 1, 2])` returns `[3, nan, 1, 2]`: not sorted at all. Filter NaNs out first or use a key that places them explicitly.
- Comparators that read mutable state (a "current time" or a cache that changes mid-sort).

## Key takeaways
- Strict weak ordering includes transitivity of both ordering and incomparability.
- Overflow, NaNs and changing state can break the contract and invalidate sorting results.

## Further reading
- [Comparator contract — Java documentation](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/Comparator.html)
- [Ordering requirements — C++ working draft](https://eel.is/c++draft/alg.sorting)

3. The comparator therefore says a < b, which is false. Meanwhile it says a > 0 and 0 > b, so transitivity breaks.
4. TimSort may notice the contradiction and throw `IllegalArgumentException`, or silently produce a wrong order.

options.text: `<=` returns true for equal elements, violating irreflexivity (comp(a, a) must be false); this is undefined behaviour, and the unguarded inner loops can run past the end of the array

2. With `<=`, comp(x, x) is true for every x. Violating the requirement is undefined behaviour.
3. In practice, libstdc++'s partition and final insertion sort use *unguarded* loops such as "move left while comp(val, *prev)". They assume a pivot or sentinel will stop them. With `<=` and duplicate values, the sentinel doesn't stop the loop, and it reads before the start or past the end of the vector.
4. Result: reads and writes out of bounds, which may crash or corrupt memory only on some inputs.

Fix: use `<` (or `std::less<>()`).

lessons.title: Key functions and cached work
lessons.summary: A key function is evaluated once per element.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Keys instead of comparators

Python 3 dropped `cmp` in favour of `key`. A key function is called **once per element**: n calls. A comparator is called on every comparison: O(n log n) calls in the worst case for this sort, often fewer on ordered inputs. For a million items that is 1 million versus 20 million calls to an expensive function, such as lower-casing a string or parsing a date.

This is a caller-context excerpt: `rows` contains objects with country and score fields.

```python
# Group countries; rank scores descending.
rows.sort(
    key=lambda r: (r.country, -r.score))
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: weighing parcels once and writing it on a sticker
> To line up a pile of parcels by weight, you could put two parcels on the scales every time you compare them, weighing the same parcel again and again. Or you could weigh each parcel once, write the weight on a sticker, and compare stickers.
>
> **How it maps:** weighing is the expensive key computation (lower-casing, parsing a date), the sticker is the cached key, and comparing stickers is the cheap comparison the sort repeats many times. Weighing in every comparison is the comparator approach.
>
> **Where it stops:** stickers take a little space, and the same is true in code: a key function stores one computed key per element, so it trades some memory for far fewer expensive calls.

The saving costs some memory: CPython keeps the n computed keys in a separate array for the duration of the sort. This "decorate, sort, undecorate" pattern is known as the **Schwartzian transform** from Perl. Tuple keys give lexicographic multi-field order. When a field cannot be negated (strings in descending order), use `functools.cmp_to_key` or rely on stability.

## Key takeaways
- A key function is evaluated once per element.
- Tuple keys express lexicographic order and avoid repeating expensive transformations in every comparison.

## Further reading
- [Sorting techniques — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html)
- [CPython 3.14.0 list-sort design notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/listsort.txt)

options.explanation: Correct. A key function runs once per element (1 million calls). A comparator runs once per comparison (about 20 million), lower-casing two strings each time.

options.text: Both about 1 million

2. **Comparator:** each of the roughly 20 million comparisons calls `cmp(a, b)`, which lower-cases both strings again: about 40 million calls.

That's roughly 40× more work in the expensive function. The key approach is the Schwartzian transform (decorate, sort, undecorate), and it's why Python 3 dropped `cmp`.

lessons.title: Stable multi-key sorting and pagination
lessons.summary: Sort secondary keys first, then primary keys with a stable algorithm.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Stability in practice

Stability lets you build multi-key sorts from single-key sorts. **Sort by the secondary key first, then by the primary key:**

```python
people = [("ann", 30), ("bob", 25),
          ("cat", 30), ("dan", 25)]
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[0])  # name
people.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])  # age
# [('bob',25), ('dan',25),
#  ('ann',30), ('cat',30)]
```

The second sort orders by age; within equal ages, the stable sort keeps the name order from the first sort. This is exactly how clicking "sort by name" and then "sort by age" behaves in a spreadsheet or UI table: users expect the earlier ordering to survive within ties, and an unstable sort makes rows jump around.

Python's `reverse=True` is also stable: equal elements keep their original order rather than being reversed.

> [!tip] Choosing in practice
> Use your language's default sort with a key function. Reach for a stable sort when the order of ties is visible to users or downstream code. Reach for an unstable one (`sort_unstable`, `std::sort`) only when you have measured that sorting matters and ties are indistinguishable.

JavaScript’s default `Array.sort()` compares string conversions when no comparator is supplied: `[10, 9, 1].sort()` becomes `[1, 10, 9]`. Use a numeric comparator for numeric order. A database pagination query also needs a deterministic tie-breaker such as a unique order ID after its date; a stable in-memory algorithm cannot add a missing SQL ordering key.


## Key takeaways
- Sort secondary keys first, then primary keys with a stable algorithm.
- Pagination additionally needs a deterministic total order, usually a unique tie-breaker.

## Further reading
- [Sorting techniques — Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html)
- [CPython 3.14.0 list-sort design notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/v3.14.0/Objects/listsort.txt)

No ordering, numeric or string, puts 9 first and 1 last.

```

-> [1, 10, 9]
```

3. For numbers, always pass a comparator: `.sort((a, b) => a - b)` gives `[1, 9, 10]`. (Subtraction is safe for ordinary JS numbers, which are doubles, but avoid it with NaN.)

lessons.title: Binary search from a closed invariant
lessons.summary: Each probe shrinks the candidate range by roughly half.
lessons.body:
Binary search is the payoff for sorting. Throughout this lesson, n is the number of elements in the sorted array, and costs use Big O notation (O(log n) grows with the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times n can be halved before reaching 1). In a sorted array of a billion items, it finds any key in at most 30 middle-element probes. The Python code may perform both equality and order tests per probe. The idea fits in a sentence: compare with the middle element and discard the half that cannot contain the answer.

And yet it is notoriously easy to get wrong. Jon Bentley reported that when he asked professional programmers to write it, around 90% of their versions had bugs. The fix is not to memorise a template, but to write every binary search from an explicit **invariant**.

## Why it is fast

Each probe halves the range of candidates. The search ends when one or zero candidates remain, so the number of probes is the number of times n can be halved before reaching 1:

```formula essential
r_k ≈ n / 2^k
r_k ≈ 1  when  k ≈ log_2(n)
where
r_k: how many elements are still in range after k probes
n: the number of elements in the sorted array
k: the number of probes taken so far
2^k: 2 multiplied by itself k times
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: how many halvings take n down to 1
≈: approximately equal to
In words: every probe halves what is left, so the number of probes grows with the logarithm of the array size: doubling the array adds only one probe.
```

| n | max comparisons |
|---|---|
| 1,000 | 10 |
| 1,000,000 | 20 |
| 1,000,000,000 | 30 |

Precisely, a successful search needs at most one probe per halving plus one for the last remaining element. The decision-tree argument from the lower-bound units in this module shows no comparison-based search can do better in the worst case.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: finding a word in a printed dictionary
> To find "otter" in a dictionary, open it near the middle. If the page shows words starting with "m", every page before it is ruled out, so you only ever look in the back half. Open the middle of that half, and so on. A thousand-page dictionary takes only about ten openings.
>
> **How it maps:** the pages still in play are the range `[lo, hi]`, opening the middle page is probing `mid`, and discarding the half that cannot contain the word is moving `lo` or `hi` past `mid`.
>
> **Where it stops:** people open a dictionary near where they expect the word ("o" is past the middle), which is interpolation search rather than binary search. And it only works because the dictionary is in alphabetical order; binary search on data that is not sorted by the same rule returns nonsense without any warning.

## Think in invariants

Write down what is true about `lo` and `hi` before every iteration, and make sure each update keeps it true. The loop condition and the return value then follow.

### Version 1: find any index of x (closed interval)

Here `a` is the sorted array, n its length, x the value we are looking for, and `lo` and `hi` the indices bounding the part of the array still in play.

**Invariant:** if x is in the array, it is in `a[lo..hi]` (inclusive).

```python
def search(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:      # range non-empty
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        # A matching midpoint ends this
        # search.
        if a[mid] == x:
            return mid
        # All keys through mid are too
        # small.
        if a[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1  # x right of mid
        else:
            hi = mid - 1  # x is left of mid
    return -1
```

Every choice follows from the invariant. The range `[lo, hi]` is empty when `lo > hi`, so loop while `lo <= hi`. When `a[mid] < x`, mid itself is ruled out, so `lo = mid + 1`, not `mid`.

## Key takeaways
- Each probe shrinks the candidate range by roughly half.
- Closed intervals require an inclusive loop and updates strictly beyond a rejected midpoint.

## Further reading
- [Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html)

lessons.title: Insertion bounds, counts and duplicates
lessons.summary: The lower bound is the first not-less position and the upper bound the first greater position.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

### Version 2: lower_bound (half-open interval)

Finding *some* match is often not enough. You want the **first** position where x could go: the **binary-search lower bound** (often called lower_bound), the index of the first element at least as large as the search value. This is what Python's `bisect_left` and C++'s `std::lower_bound` return.

**Invariant:** all elements before `lo` are smaller than the search value, and all elements at or beyond `hi` are at least the search value. The candidate insertion indices include both endpoints, even though the remaining element range excludes `hi`.

```python
def lower_bound(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        # All keys through mid are too
        # small.
        if a[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1   # a[mid] < x
        else:
            # Keep mid as a possible
            # insertion point.
            hi = mid       # a[mid] >= x
    return lo
```

When the endpoints meet, every preceding key is smaller than the search value and every following key is at least that value. That is the answer by definition. Note `hi = len(a)`, not `len(a) - 1`: the answer can be "after everything".

Trace: find lower_bound of 8 in `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13]`.

```
lo hi mid a[mid]
0  7  3   7    7 < 8   -> lo = 4
4  7  5   11   11 >= 8 -> hi = 5
4  5  4   9    9 >= 8  -> hi = 4
lo == hi == 4: insert 8 at index 4
```

The **binary-search upper bound** (upper_bound: the first element > x, `bisect_right`) is identical except the test becomes `a[mid] <= x`.

```
input: [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8]
target 3: lower result 1, upper result 4
three copies: 4 - 1 = 3
target 4: both results 4; zero copies
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: shelving another copy of a book
> A library shelf holds three copies of the same title among other books in title order. A new copy could go just before the existing copies or just after them; both keep the shelf in order. The gap between those two spots is exactly the three existing copies.
>
> **How it maps:** "just before the copies" is the binary-search lower bound (the first book not earlier than the title), "just after" is the binary-search upper bound (the first book later than it), and the distance between them counts the equal keys. If the title is not on the shelf, both spots are the same place.
>
> **Where it stops:** on a real shelf you can push books aside to make room. In an array, inserting at the found position still means shifting every later element, so finding the spot is logarithmic but inserting is linear.

lower_bound and upper_bound together answer most real questions: does x exist (`lo < n and a[lo] == x`), how many copies, where to insert while keeping order, and range queries ("all orders between 10:00 and 11:00" is `[lower_bound(10:00), lower_bound(11:00))`).

Java’s `Arrays.binarySearch` returns a match index if present. If absent, its negative result encodes the insertion point: negate the insertion point and subtract one. For `[10, 20, 30, 40]`, searching for 25 has insertion point 2 and returns −3.


For a nearest-value query, inspect the lower-bound position and the position immediately before it, when they exist. One is the first not-less value and the other the largest smaller value, so a closer candidate cannot hide farther away. Return the smaller absolute distance; decide how ties should be broken. A count over a value interval likewise comes from subtracting its two insertion-bound indices, rather than scanning every matching element.

## Key takeaways
- The lower bound is the first not-less position and the upper bound the first greater position.
- Their difference counts equal keys, and insertion positions may be after the entire array.

## Further reading
- [Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html)

lessons.title: Binary-search progress and overflow
lessons.summary: Avoid overflowing fixed-width midpoint arithmetic.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## The classic pitfalls

### 1. Midpoint overflow

The following Java lines are alternative midpoint expressions, not three declarations to place in one scope.

```java
int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;        // bug
int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;   // fix
int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;      // Java
```

A 32-bit signed `int` can hold values only up to 2,147,483,647 (about 2.1 billion). Two large indices can add up to more than that: with `lo` at 1.1 billion and `hi` at 1.2 billion, the sum is 2.3 billion, which wraps round to a negative number. The safe form only ever adds half the gap to `lo`, so its result never exceeds `hi` and cannot overflow.

For nonnegative Java int indices, the addition `lo + hi` can wrap once the array has more than about a billion elements, producing a negative midpoint. Signed overflow in C and C++ is undefined behavior; other languages have their own checked, wrapping or unsigned rules. In 2006 Joshua Bloch revealed that this bug had sat in Java's `Arrays.binarySearch` for about nine years, and in the version in Programming Pearls for two decades. Python's integers do not overflow, but C, C++, Java, Go and Rust code must use the safe form.

### 2. Infinite loops

If you ever write `lo = mid`, check what happens when `hi = lo + 1`. Then the rounded-down midpoint is `lo` itself (for `lo` 4 and `hi` 5, `(4 + 5) // 2` is 4), so `lo = mid` changes nothing and the loop spins forever:

```
lo 4, hi 5 -> mid 4 -> lo = mid = 4
lo 4, hi 5 -> mid 4 -> ... forever
```

The fixes: make every branch move strictly past mid (`lo = mid + 1`), or round the midpoint up (`mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2`) when the branch is `lo = mid`, or loop while `hi - lo > 1` (see the later integer-root unit).

### 3. Mixing interval conventions

Most bugs come from mixing closed `[lo, hi]` and half-open `[lo, hi)` conventions: `hi = len(a)` with `while lo <= hi` reads past the end; `hi = len(a) - 1` with `hi = mid` can never return n. Pick one convention per function and derive every line from it.

### 4. Unsorted or wrongly sorted input

Binary search on data that is not sorted by the same ordering silently returns nonsense, not an error. Sorting by `key=str.lower` and then searching with raw strings is a classic mismatch.

> [!tip] Test the edges
> Every binary search should be tested on: an empty array, one element, x smaller than everything, x larger than everything, x absent but in the middle, and many duplicates. Off-by-one bugs hide in exactly those cases.

## Key takeaways
- Avoid overflowing fixed-width midpoint arithmetic.
- Derive termination and updates from one interval convention and test empty, absent and duplicate cases.

## Further reading
- [Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html)

lessons.title: Searching rotated arrays
lessons.summary: With distinct keys, at least one midpoint half is sorted.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Searching a rotated sorted array

A sorted array rotated at an unknown point, like `[15, 18, 22, 3, 6, 9, 12]`, is not sorted, but **at least one half around any mid is sorted**. Check which half is sorted and whether x lies inside its range.

```python
def search_rotated(a, x):  # distinct keys
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        # A matching midpoint ends this
        # search.
        if a[mid] == x:
            return mid
        # Distinct keys reveal a sorted
        # half.
        if a[lo] <= a[mid]:  # left sorted
            if a[lo] <= x < a[mid]:
                hi = mid - 1
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        else:  # right half sorted
            if a[mid] < x <= a[hi]:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid - 1
    return -1
```

This is still O(log n), but only for **distinct** keys. With duplicates, `[2, 2, 2, 3, 2]` makes it impossible to tell which half is sorted when `a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi]`, and the worst case becomes O(n).

The same idea finds the **rotation point** (the minimum): if `a[mid] > a[hi]`, the drop is to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to its left.

## Key takeaways
- With distinct keys, at least one midpoint half is sorted.
- Equal endpoints can hide the rotation and force linear worst-case work.

## Further reading
- [Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html)

lessons.title: Monotone feasibility and shipping capacity
lessons.summary: Feasibility must be monotone and cheap enough to evaluate.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Binary search on the answer

The most powerful generalisation: you do not need an array at all. You need a **monotone predicate**: a yes/no test that is false up to some point and true from then on.

```
cap:     10 11 12 13 14 15 16 ...
ok?:      F  F  F  F  F  T  T ...
                         ^ find this
```

Binary search finds the first true by evaluating the predicate only a logarithmic number of times: each evaluation halves the range of candidate answers, so 46 candidates need at most 6 checks, and a billion need about 30.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: choosing the smallest removal van
> Moving house, you want the smallest van that fits everything. Van sizes form a ladder, and if a size fits, every bigger size fits too. So rather than trying every size in turn, you test the middle size: if it fits, look smaller; if not, look bigger. A handful of trial packings finds the answer.
>
> **How it maps:** van sizes are the candidate answers, "does everything fit?" is the monotone predicate, a trial packing is the feasibility check, and halving the ladder after each trial is binary search on the answer.
>
> **Where it stops:** real trial packings are slow and tiring; the trick only pays off in code when the check is cheap enough to run many times and is *exactly* monotone. If a bigger size could ever fail where a smaller one worked, binary search can return a wrong answer without warning.

**Example.** Packages with weights `[1, 2, ..., 10]` must be shipped in order within 5 days. What is the minimum ship capacity that works?

- A ship capacity below 10 cannot carry the heaviest package; 55 (the total) does it in one day. So the answer is in `[10, 55]`.
- "Can we ship with capacity c?" is monotone: if c works, any larger c works. It is checked greedily in O(n).

```python
def can_ship(w, days, cap):
    if days < 1:
        return False
    need, load = 1, 0
    for x in w:
        if x > cap:
            return False
        # A full ship starts the next
        # ordered day.
        if load + x > cap:
            need += 1   # start a new day
            load = 0
        load += x
    return need <= days

def min_capacity(w, days):
    if days < 1 or not w:
        raise ValueError("weights and days")
    if any(type(x) is not int or x <= 0
           for x in w):
        raise ValueError(
            "positive int weights"
        )
    lo, hi = max(w), sum(w)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        # Feasible capacity may still be too
        # large.
        if can_ship(w, days, mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo
```

```
lo  hi  mid  ok?
10  55  32   yes -> hi = 32
10  32  21   yes -> hi = 21
10  21  15   yes -> hi = 15
10  15  12   no  -> lo = 13
13  15  14   no  -> lo = 15
answer: 15
```

Five checks of O(n) each, instead of trying all 46 capacities. In general:

```formula essential
T = O(n log(S))
where
T: the total running time of min_capacity
n: the number of packages; each feasibility check walks all of them once
S: the total weight of all packages, which bounds the range of capacities to search (55 here)
log: the logarithm (base 2 here; the base only changes a constant)
O: Big O: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor
In words: about log(S) feasibility checks, each costing one pass over the n packages.
```

Because S sits inside a logarithm, a much heavier load barely changes the work: multiplying the total weight by 1,000 adds only about 10 more checks. More packages, on the other hand, make every check longer.

The same pattern handles largest minimum separation of routers when feasibility is monotone and efficiently checkable. It needs both properties: a job-scheduling decision can be monotone yet computationally hard to check, and a predicate that is not reliably monotone gives no guarantee at all.

## Key takeaways
- Feasibility must be monotone and cheap enough to evaluate.
- Shipping capacity uses a greedy ordered pass inside each binary-search check.

## Further reading
- [Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html)

lessons.title: Integer square roots and search applications
lessons.summary: A feasible lower endpoint and infeasible upper endpoint converge to the integer root.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding search units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

**Integer square root** is another instance, using the `hi - lo > 1` style:

```python
def isqrt(n):
    if type(n) is not int or n < 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "nonnegative integer"
        )
    lo, hi = 0, n + 1   # lo*lo <= n < hi*hi
    while hi - lo > 1:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        # Keep a feasible floor-root
        # candidate.
        if mid * mid <= n:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo
```

For **real-valued** answers, use a suitable tolerance and an iteration limit, and stop when the computed midpoint equals an endpoint. A fixed 100 halvings does not cover every possible binary64 interval, especially across large exponent ranges or near subnormal values.

## Binary search in the wild

- **`git bisect`** narrows commit ancestry using good/bad tests. On a linear, monotone history with no skipped commits, 1,000 candidates take about 10 tests; merge graphs, flaky tests and fixes/reintroductions complicate that model.
- **B-tree pages** in databases (PostgreSQL, InnoDB) binary search the sorted keys inside each page.
- **Timsort's galloping** (covered earlier in this module) is an exponential search: probe 1, 3, 7, 15 ... until overshooting, then binary search. That is the right tool when the answer is probably near the start or the range is unbounded.
- **Standard libraries:** Python's `bisect`, C++'s `lower_bound`, `upper_bound` and `equal_range`, Java's `Arrays.binarySearch` (returns `-(insertion point) - 1` when absent), and Go's `sort.Search`, which is binary search on a predicate.

## Key takeaways
- A feasible lower endpoint and infeasible upper endpoint converge to the integer root.
- Library and real-valued searches require their own ordering, rounding and termination contracts.

## Further reading
- [Insertion-bound searches — Python bisect](https://docs.python.org/3/library/bisect.html)
- [Integer square-root contract — Python math](https://docs.python.org/3/library/math.html#math.isqrt)

lessons.title: Selection ranks and tournament minima
lessons.summary: Selection asks for ranks rather than an entirely sorted array.
lessons.body:
Many questions that sound like sorting are really selection problems, answered by a **selection algorithm**: find the median latency, the 99th percentile, the 10 highest-scoring posts, the k nearest points. You need one element (or k elements) in the right place, not the whole array ordered.

Sorting answers all of these in O(n log n). But selection can be done in **O(n)**, and top-k in **O(n log(k + 1))**. At a billion items, the base-two logarithm of the input size is about thirty; this compares asymptotic growth, not literal pass counts or measured runtime.

Throughout, n is the number of elements, costs use Big O notation (how a cost grows with n, ignoring constant factors), and "k-th smallest" is 0-based: rank zero is the minimum, the last rank is the maximum, and the integer-divided halfway index is the upper middle value for even-length inputs. The numeric median of an even sample conventionally averages its two central values.

## The easy cases

- **Minimum or maximum**: one pass, one fewer comparison than the number of items. That is optimal: every element except the winner must lose at least one comparison.
- **Min and max together**: compare elements in pairs, then the smaller with the current min and the larger with the current max. That is about one and a half comparisons per element instead of two.
- **Second smallest**: a knockout tournament finds it with only a few extra comparisons. The runner-up must have lost directly to the winner, and the winner played only about a logarithmic number of matches, so a second small contest among the players the winner beat finds it.

```formula reference
C_min = n − 1
C_mm ≈ 3n / 2
C_2 ≤ n + ⌈log_2(n)⌉ − 2
where
C_min: the comparisons needed to find the minimum (or the maximum) alone
C_mm: the comparisons needed to find the minimum and maximum together, using pairs
C_2: the comparisons a balanced knockout tournament uses to find the second smallest, for at least two distinct items; the displayed upper bound is exact when n is a power of two
n: the number of elements
log_2(n): the base-2 logarithm of n: the number of rounds in a knockout tournament of n players (10 for 1,024)
⌈ ⌉: the ceiling: round up to the next whole number
≈: approximately equal to
≤: less than or equal to
In words: the minimum needs one comparison per loser; doing min and max together saves about a quarter; the runner-up costs only about as many extra comparisons as the winner played matches.
```

For 1,024 elements: 1,023 comparisons for the minimum, about 1,536 for min and max together instead of 2,046 separately, and 1,032 for the second smallest.

The general k is where it gets interesting.

## Key takeaways
- Selection asks for ranks rather than an entirely sorted array.
- Tournament losers prove minimum and second-minimum comparison costs.

## Further reading
- [Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)

options.explanation: That's the cost of binary search on *sorted* data. With unsorted data every element must be checked.

options.text: The input size times its base-two logarithm
options.explanation: That's the cost of sorting, far more than needed to find just the minimum.

options.explanation: Half the elements would never be looked at, and the minimum could be among them.

1. **Upper bound:** scan once keeping the smallest so far: one fewer comparison than the number of items (999 for 1,000 numbers).
2. **Lower bound:** to be sure x is the minimum, every other element must have been shown to be larger than something. Each comparison has exactly one loser, so producing a loser for every element except the winner takes at least one fewer comparison than the number of items.

So one fewer comparison than the input size is optimal. Finding the minimum and maximum together needs only about one and a half comparisons per input item (about 1,500 for 1,000 numbers) instead of about two per item, by comparing elements in pairs first.

lessons.title: Quickselect keeps one partition
lessons.summary: Only the side containing the requested rank survives.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Quickselect

Hoare's **quickselect** (1961) is quicksort that only recurses into **one side**. Partition around a pivot. The pivot lands at its final index p. If p equals k, done. If k is smaller than p, the answer is on the left; otherwise it is on the right. Throw the other side away.

```python
import random

def quickselect(a, k):
    if not 0 <= k < len(a):
        raise IndexError(
            "rank out of range"
        )
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while True:
        if lo == hi:
            return a[lo]
        # Uniform pivot choice gives
        # expectation.
        r = random.randint(lo, hi)
        a[r], a[hi] = a[hi], a[r]
        # Partition before choosing the next
        # range.
        p = lomuto(a, lo, hi)
        # The desired global index is now
        # fixed.
        if k == p:
            return a[p]
        # Only retain the side with the
        # wanted rank.
        if k < p:
            # Discard the pivot and its
            # right side.
            hi = p - 1
        else:
            # Discard the pivot and its left
            # side.
            lo = p + 1
```

(`lomuto` is the partition from the quicksort lesson.) This compact version has the expected linear guarantee for distinct keys. With duplicates, random pivots alone do not prevent quadratic time on all-equal input; use a three-way partition and discard the entire equal block for a duplicate-robust version. Because only one side survives, recursion becomes a loop.

Trace with the last element as pivot (no randomisation, to keep it readable), finding k = 5 in `[7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4]`:

```
pivot 4: [2,1,3,4,8,5,7,6]  p 3
k=5 > 3: keep a[4..7] = [8,5,7,6]
pivot 6: [5,6,7,8]          p 5
k == p: answer 6
```

Check: sorted, the array is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]` and index 5 is 6.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: finding the 10th-cheapest flat
> You want the 10th-cheapest flat from 200 listings. Pick one listing as a reference and split the rest into a cheaper pile and a pricier pile. If the cheaper pile holds 25 listings, the 10th-cheapest must be in it, so you never look at the pricier pile again. Repeat with a new reference inside the pile you kept.
>
> **How it maps:** the reference listing is the pivot, splitting into piles is the partition, and keeping only the pile that contains the wanted position is quickselect discarding one side. Nobody ever puts the piles in full price order, which is the saving over sorting.
>
> **Where it stops:** a person would pick a reference that looks typically priced. Quickselect picks blindly (at random), so an unlucky pick can be the cheapest or dearest listing and remove only itself; a long run of such picks is what makes the worst case quadratic.

### Why it is expected O(n)

With a good pivot, each round discards a constant fraction. If every pivot split the array in half, the work would be a **geometric series** (each term a fixed fraction of the one before):

```formula essential
W = n + n / 2 + n / 4 + … ≤ 2n
where
W: the total number of elements partitioned over all rounds
n: the number of elements
…: "and so on", each term half the one before
≤: less than or equal to
In words: halving the work every round adds up to less than twice the first round's work, so the total is linear.
```

So the total is linear. For distinct keys, with random pivots the splits are not exactly half, but the pivot lands in the middle 50% of the range with probability 1/2, and then at least a quarter is discarded. The expected cost is still a geometric series: **O(n)**. A more careful analysis puts the expected cost of finding the median at about 3.4 comparisons per element, and less for ranks near either end:

```formula reference
C ≈ 2(1 + ln(2))n
C ≈ 3.39n
where
C: the expected comparisons randomised quickselect makes to find the median of n distinct keys
n: the number of elements
ln(2): the natural logarithm of 2 (base e, about 2.718), about 0.693
≈: approximately equal to (leading term)
In words: finding the median with random pivots takes about 3.4 comparisons per element on average.
```

### The worst case

Bad pivots every round shrink the range by only one element, exactly like quicksort. The rounds then partition all n elements, then one fewer, then one fewer again, down to 1: a shrinking triangle of work that adds up to about half of n squared element visits, which is **O(n²)**.

With a first- or last-element pivot, a sorted input does this. Random pivots make it vanishingly unlikely, but not impossible, and an adversary who can predict your random number generator can still force it.

## Key takeaways
- Only the side containing the requested rank survives.
- Independent random pivots give expected linear work for distinct keys; poor splits still give a quadratic worst case.

## Further reading
- [Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)
- [Time bounds for selection — Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan](https://people.csail.mit.edu/rivest/pubs/BFPRT73.pdf)
- [Quickselect comparison analysis — Martínez and Roura](https://www.cs.upc.edu/~conrado/research/papers/sicomp-mr01.pdf)

**Worst:** every pivot is the smallest or largest remaining element, so each round removes only the pivot. The rounds then partition every element, then one fewer, then one fewer again, down to 1: a triangle of about half of n squared, which is quadratic.

lessons.title: Median-of-medians pivot guarantees
lessons.summary: Groups of five guarantee a fixed fraction on each side, allowing rounding corrections.
lessons.body:
This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise.

## Median of medians: worst-case O(n)

In 1973 Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan showed that selection can be done in O(n) **guaranteed**. The trick is to spend a little linear work finding a pivot that is provably not too far from the middle.

1. Split the array into groups of 5.
2. Find the median of each group (constant work per group).
3. **Recursively** select the median of the group medians (one per five items, rounded up). Use it as the pivot.
4. Partition and recurse into the side containing k.

```python
def select(a, k):
    if not 0 <= k < len(a):
        raise IndexError(
            "rank out of range"
        )
    if len(a) <= 5:
        return sorted(a)[k]
    groups = [a[i:i + 5]
              for i in range(0, len(a), 5)]
    medians = [sorted(g)[len(g) // 2]
               for g in groups]
    mid = len(medians) // 2
    # Recursively find a well-balanced
    # pivot.
    pivot = select(medians, mid)
    lows = [x for x in a if x < pivot]
    highs = [x for x in a if x > pivot]
    # Count equal keys without another
    # array.
    n_eq = len(a) - len(lows) - len(highs)
    if k < len(lows):
        return select(lows, k)
    # Every rank in the equal block is
    # pivot.
    if k < len(lows) + n_eq:
        return pivot
    return select(highs,
                  k - len(lows) - n_eq)
```

### Why the pivot is good

Picture the groups as columns, each sorted with its median in the middle row, and the columns ordered by their medians. M is the median of medians.

```
 smaller medians    larger medians
   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
   m  m  m  M  m  m  m
   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
   .  .  .  |  .  .  .
```

Half of the medians are no larger than the chosen median M. Each of those medians has two more elements in its group below it. So at least 3 elements in each of about half the groups are no bigger than M, and by symmetry the same number are no smaller:

```formula reference
s ≥ 3n / 10 − 6
r ≤ 7n / 10 + 6
where
s: the number of elements guaranteed to be no bigger than M (and, by symmetry, no smaller than M)
M: the median of the group medians, used as the pivot
n: the number of elements
r: the most elements the recursive call in step 4 can receive
≥: greater than or equal to
≤: less than or equal to
In words: three elements from each of half the groups lie on each side of M, so at least about 30% of the input is discarded every round and the recursive call gets at most about 70%; the small constant allows for the ragged last group and M's own group.
```

For 1,000 elements the conservative finite bound excludes at least 294 and leaves at most 706 for the retained recursive side, whatever the input order.

That gives two recursive calls per round: one on the group medians (a fifth of the input) to choose the pivot, and one on the retained side (at most about seven tenths). Together they handle at most about **nine tenths** of the input, so each level of recursion does at most about 90% of the previous level's work.

```formula reference
T(n) ≤ T(⌈n / 5⌉) + T(r) + cn
r ≤ 7n / 10 + 6
1/5 + 7/10 = 9/10
T(n) = O(n)
where
T(n): the worst-case running time of median of medians on n elements
n: the number of elements
r: size of the retained recursive side
c: a fixed per-element upper bound on grouping and partition work, in operations per element
⌈ ⌉: ceiling, round upward for the ragged group
O: Big O: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor
≤: less than or equal to
In words: the pivot search and the retained side together receive about nine tenths of the input, apart from small rounding allowances, so the work shrinks geometrically from level to level and the total is linear.
```

Ignoring constant rounding allowances for the asymptotic argument, the two recursive size fractions sum to nine tenths, which is less than one. The total work at each level of recursion shrinks geometrically, and the whole algorithm is **O(n)**.

> [!note] Why groups of 5?
> With groups of 3, the guarantee is only about a third on each side. The pivot search then gets a third of the input and the retained side up to two thirds: together the whole input, so the work no longer shrinks from level to level and this analysis establishes only O(n log n), not a matching lower bound. Five is the smallest odd group size giving linear time by this simple argument; other algorithms can use repeated grouping or different methods.

## Key takeaways
- Groups of five guarantee a fixed fraction on each side, allowing rounding corrections.
- Selecting the medians and the retained side together uses less than the whole input per asymptotic level.

## Further reading
- [Heap operations and top-k — Python heapq](https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)
- [Time bounds for selection — Blum, Floyd, Pratt, Rivest and Tarjan](https://people.csail.mit.edu/rivest/pubs/BFPRT73.pdf)
